title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: "My dear Boris," said Princess Anna Mikhaylovna to her son as Countess Rostova's carriage, in which they were riding, rolled over the straw-covered street and turned into the wide courtyard of Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov's mansion. "My dear Boris," said the mother, drawing her hand from beneath her old cloak and laying it timidly and tenderly on her son's arm, "be warm and attentive to him. Count Kirill Vladimirovich is your godfather, after all, and your future depends on him. Remember that, my dear, and be as charming as you know how to be."
"If I thought anything besides humiliation would come of it..." her son replied coldly. "But I promised, and I'll do it for your sake."

Although the hall porter could see someone's carriage standing at the entrance, after sizing up the mother and son — who had walked straight through the glass vestibule between the rows of statues in niches without asking to be announced — and casting a meaningful look at the lady's old cloak, he asked whether they wanted to see the count or the princesses. When he heard they wished to see the count, he said his excellency was worse today and was not receiving anyone.
"[Speaking in French] We might as well go back," said the son.
"My dear!" his mother exclaimed imploringly, laying her hand on his arm again as if that touch could both soothe and strengthen him.
Boris said nothing more but looked at his mother questioningly, without removing his cloak.

"My friend," Anna Mikhaylovna said gently, addressing the hall porter, "I know Count Kirill Vladimirovich is very ill... that's exactly why I've come. I'm a relative. I won't disturb him, my friend... I only need to see Prince Vasili Sergeevich — he's staying here, isn't he? Please announce me."
The hall porter sullenly pulled a bell that rang upstairs and turned away.

"Princess Drubetskaya to see Prince Vasili Sergeevich," he called to a footman dressed in knee breeches, buckled shoes, and a tailcoat, who came running down the stairs and peered over from the halfway landing.
The mother smoothed the folds of her faded silk dress in front of a large Venetian mirror on the wall and, in her worn-down shoes, briskly climbed the carpeted staircase.
"My dear," she said to her son, rallying him once more with a touch, "you promised me!"
The son, lowering his eyes, followed her quietly.
They entered the large hall, from which one of the doors led to Prince Vasili's apartments.

Just as the mother and son reached the middle of the hall and were about to ask directions from an elderly footman who had jumped up when they entered, the bronze handle of one of the doors turned and Prince Vasili emerged — wearing a velvet coat with a single star on his chest, as he always did at home — saying goodbye to a good-looking, dark-haired man. This was the celebrated Petersburg doctor, Lorrain.
"So it's certain?" said the prince.
"Prince, to err is human, but..." replied the doctor, swallowing his r's and pronouncing the Latin words with a French accent.
The original Latin footnote: To err is human.
"Very well, very well..."

Seeing Anna Mikhaylovna and her son, Prince Vasili dismissed the doctor with a bow and approached them silently, with a questioning look. The son noticed that a look of deep sorrow suddenly crossed his mother's face, and he smiled faintly.
"Ah, Prince! What sad circumstances bring us together again! And how is our dear patient?" she said, as though unaware of the cold, hostile stare directed at her.

Prince Vasili looked at her and at Boris, puzzled and wary. Boris bowed politely. Prince Vasili, without acknowledging the bow, turned to Anna Mikhaylovna and answered her question with a movement of his head and lips that indicated very little hope for the patient.
"Is it possible?" Anna Mikhaylovna exclaimed. "Oh, how terrible! It's dreadful to think... This is my son," she added, indicating Boris. "He wanted to thank you personally."
Boris bowed politely again.
"Believe me, Prince, a mother's heart will never forget what you've done for us."

"I'm glad I was able to be of service, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna," said Prince Vasili, adjusting his lace cravat. His tone and manner here in Moscow, with Anna Mikhaylovna whom he had placed under an obligation, carried far more self-importance than it had at Anna Pavlovna's reception in Petersburg.
"Try to serve well and show yourself worthy," he added, turning to Boris with severity. "I'm glad... Are you here on leave?" he went on, reverting to his usual tone of indifference.

"I'm awaiting orders to join my new regiment, your excellency," Boris replied, showing neither annoyance at the prince's curt manner nor eagerness to engage in conversation, but speaking so quietly and respectfully that the prince gave him a searching look.
"Are you living with your mother?"
"I'm staying with Countess Rostova," Boris replied, again adding, "your excellency."
"That is, with Ilya Rostov, who married Natalia Shinshina," Anna Mikhaylovna clarified.

"I know, I know," Prince Vasili answered in his monotonous voice. "I could never understand how Natalia brought herself to marry that uncouth bear! A perfectly absurd and stupid man, and a gambler too, I'm told."

"But a very kind man, Prince," said Anna Mikhaylovna with a sympathetic smile, as though she too knew Count Rostov deserved the criticism but was asking the prince not to be too hard on the poor old fellow. "What do the doctors say?" she asked after a pause, her worn face once again expressing deep sorrow.
"They give little hope," replied the prince.
"And I did so want to thank Uncle for all his kindness to me and Boris. He is Boris's godfather," she added, her tone implying that this fact should give Prince Vasili considerable satisfaction.
Prince Vasili grew thoughtful and frowned. Anna Mikhaylovna could see he was afraid of finding a rival for Count Bezukhov's fortune, and she hurried to reassure him.

"If it weren't for my sincere affection and devotion to Uncle," she said — pronouncing the word with studied confidence and nonchalance — "I know his character: noble, upright... but you see, he has no one with him except the young princesses... They're still young..." She lowered her head and continued in a whisper: "Has he fulfilled his final duty, Prince? How precious those last moments are! It can't make things any worse, and he absolutely must be prepared, if he's so ill. We women, Prince," and she smiled tenderly, "always know how to say these things. I simply must see him, however painful it may be for me. I'm accustomed to suffering."
Clearly the prince understood her, just as he had understood at Anna Pavlovna's, that it would be very difficult to get rid of Anna Mikhaylovna.
"Wouldn't such a visit be too much for him, dear Anna Mikhaylovna?" he said. "Let's wait until this evening. The doctors are expecting a crisis."
"But one cannot delay at a moment like this, Prince! Think — the welfare of his soul is at stake. Oh, it's terrible: the duties of a Christian..."

A door from one of the inner rooms opened and one of the princesses — the count's niece — came in with a cold, stern face. Her disproportionately long torso contrasted strikingly with her short legs. Prince Vasili turned to her.
"Well, how is he?"
"The same. But what do you expect, with all this noise..." said the princess, looking at Anna Mikhaylovna as though she were a stranger.

"Ah, my dear, I hardly recognized you," said Anna Mikhaylovna with a bright smile, bustling cheerfully up to the count's niece. "I've come, and I'm here to help you nurse my uncle. I can only imagine what you've been through," she added, turning up her eyes sympathetically.

The princess said nothing, didn't even smile, and left the room. Anna Mikhaylovna removed her gloves and, having claimed her position, settled into an armchair and invited Prince Vasili to sit beside her.

"Boris," she said to her son with a smile, "I'm going in to see the count — my uncle. But you, my dear, should go find Pierre in the meantime. And don't forget to give him the Rostovs' dinner invitation. I don't suppose he'll come?" she added, turning to the prince.

"On the contrary," replied the prince, who had plainly grown gloomy, "I'd be only too grateful if you could take that young man off my hands... He's been here all this time, and the count hasn't asked for him once."
He shrugged. A footman led Boris down one flight of stairs and up another to Pierre's rooms.

title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: That same evening, a heated argument broke out among the officers in Denisov's quarters.

"I'm telling you, Rostov, you have to apologize to the colonel!" said a tall, gray-haired staff captain with an enormous mustache and deeply lined face, addressing Rostov, who was flushed red with emotion.
The staff captain, Kirsten, had been demoted to the ranks twice over matters of honor, and twice had won back his commission.

"I won't let anyone call me a liar!" Rostov burst out. "He said I was lying, and I told him he was lying. And that's where it stands. He can put me on duty every day or throw me in the brig, but nobody can force me to apologize. If he, as regimental commander, considers it beneath his dignity to give me satisfaction, then—"

"Just hold on a moment, my dear fellow, and listen," the staff captain interrupted in his deep bass voice, calmly stroking his long mustache. "You told the colonel, in front of other officers, that one of the officers had stolen—"

"It's not my fault the conversation started in front of other officers. Maybe I shouldn't have spoken in front of them, but I'm no diplomat. That's exactly why I joined the hussars—because I thought here you wouldn't need to play games. And then he tells me I'm lying, so let him give me satisfaction—"
"That's all well and good. Nobody thinks you're a coward, but that's beside the point. Ask Denisov whether it's even possible for a cadet to demand satisfaction from his regimental commander."
Denisov sat gloomily chewing his mustache, listening to the conversation with obvious reluctance to get involved. He answered the staff captain's question with a disapproving shake of his head.
"You brought up this ugly business in front of other officers," the staff captain continued, "and Bogdanich"—that was the colonel's nickname—"shut you down."
"He didn't shut me down. He said I was telling an untruth."
"Fine, have it your way. You said a lot of foolish things to him, and now you need to apologize."
"Absolutely not!" Rostov exclaimed.

"I didn't expect this from you," said the staff captain, his tone now serious and stern. "You refuse to apologize, but it's not just about him—it's about the whole regiment. All of us. You're in the wrong on every count. Here's the thing: you should have thought it through and asked for advice. But no, you went and blurted the whole thing out right in front of the officers. What was the colonel supposed to do? Have the officer court-martialed and disgrace the entire regiment? Disgrace all of us because of one scoundrel? Is that really how you see it? We don't see it that way. Bogdanich did the right thing—he told you that what you were saying wasn't true. It's not pleasant, but what else could he do, my dear fellow? You brought this on yourself. And now some kind of pride won't let you apologize, and you want to make the whole thing public. You're offended about extra duty, but why can't you apologize to an old and honorable officer? Whatever else you might think of Bogdanich, he's an honorable and brave old colonel! You're quick to take offense, but you don't mind dragging the whole regiment through the mud!" The staff captain's voice began to shake. "You've barely been with the regiment, my boy. You're here today and tomorrow you'll be posted somewhere as an adjutant, and you'll be able to shrug it off when people say, 'There are thieves among the Pavlograd officers!' But it's not the same for us! Am I right, Denisov? It's not the same!"
Denisov stayed silent and motionless, only occasionally glancing at Rostov with his glittering black eyes.

"You're too proud to apologize," the staff captain went on, "but we old fellows who've grown up in this regiment and, God willing, are going to die in it—we care about the regiment's honor. Bogdanich knows that. Yes, we care about it, old fellow! And all this isn't right—it just isn't right! You can be offended or not, but I always say what's true. It isn't right!"
The staff captain stood up and turned away from Rostov.
"That's twue, damn it all!" Denisov shouted, jumping to his feet. "Come on, Wostov, come on!"
Rostov, turning red and pale by turns, looked from one officer to the other.

"No, gentlemen, no... don't think... I understand completely. You're wrong to think that of me... I... for me... for the honor of the regiment I'd... Well, I'll prove it in battle. For me, the honor of the regiment... Well, never mind—it's true, I'm in the wrong. Completely in the wrong. So what else do you want?..."
"Now that's the spirit, Count!" the staff captain cried, turning back around and clapping Rostov on the shoulder with his big hand.
"I tell you," Denisov shouted, "he's a fine fellow!"
"That's more like it, Count," said the staff captain, now using Rostov's title as if to acknowledge his admission of fault. "Go and apologize, your excellency. Yes, go!"

"Gentlemen, I'll do anything. No one will hear another word from me," Rostov said in a pleading voice, "but I can't apologize—by God, I can't! Do whatever you want with me! How can I go and apologize like a little boy begging for forgiveness?"
Denisov started laughing.
"It'll be worse for you. Bogdanich holds grudges, and you'll pay for your stubbornness," said Kirsten.
"No, I swear it's not stubbornness! I can't explain the feeling. I just can't..."
"Well, suit yourself," said the staff captain. "And what's become of that scoundrel?" he asked Denisov.
"He's weported himself sick. He'll be stwuck off the list tomowwow," Denisov muttered.
"It's an illness—there's no other way to explain it," said the staff captain.
"Illness or not, he'd better not cwoss my path. I'd kill him!" Denisov shouted in a murderous tone.
Just then Zherkov walked into the room.
"What brings you here?" the officers called out, turning to the newcomer.
"We're going into action, gentlemen! Mack has surrendered with his entire army."
"That can't be true!"
"I've seen him with my own eyes!"
"What? You saw the actual Mack? With hands and feet and everything?"
"Into action! Into action! Someone get him a bottle for news like that! But how did you end up here?"

"I've been sent back to the regiment, all because of that devil Mack. An Austrian general complained about me. I congratulated him on Mack's arrival... What's the matter, Rostov? You look like you just stepped out of a steam bath."
"Oh, my dear fellow, we've been in such turmoil here the past two days."
The regimental adjutant came in and confirmed Zherkov's news. They had orders to advance the next day.
"We're going into action, gentlemen!"
"Thank God for that! We've been sitting around here far too long!"

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: The wind had died down and black clouds, blending with the gun smoke, hung low over the battlefield on the horizon. It was getting dark, and the glow of two fires became more visible. The cannon fire was fading, but the crackle of muskets behind them and to the right was growing louder and closer. As soon as Tushin and his guns, constantly swerving around or encountering wounded men, made it out of firing range and down into the hollow, he was met by several staff officers, including the staff officer and Zherkov, who had been sent to Tushin's battery twice but had never actually reached it. Talking over each other, they all issued orders about what to do next, scolding and blaming him. Tushin gave no orders and rode silently behind on his artillery horse, afraid to speak because he felt ready to cry at every word without knowing why. Although the orders were to leave the wounded behind, many of them dragged themselves after the troops and begged for rides on the gun carriages. The lively infantry officer who had rushed out of Tushin's hut just before the battle was now lying on 'Matvyevna's' carriage with a bullet in his stomach. At the foot of the hill, a pale hussar cadet, holding one hand with the other, came up to Tushin and asked for a seat.
"Captain, please! I've hurt my arm," he said timidly. "Please... I can't walk. Please!"
It was clear that this cadet had already asked for a ride several times and been refused. He spoke in a hesitant, pitiful voice.
"Please, give me a seat!"
"Give him a seat," said Tushin. "Lay a cloak down for him to sit on, lad," he told his favorite soldier. "And where is the wounded officer?"
"He's been put down. He died," someone answered.
"Help him up. Sit down, friend, sit down! Spread out the cloak, Antonov."

The cadet was Rostov. He was supporting one hand with the other, his face was pale and his jaw trembled with feverish shivering. They placed him on 'Matvyevna,' the gun from which the dead officer had been removed. The cloak they spread under him was wet with blood that stained his pants and arm.
"What's the matter, are you wounded, son?" said Tushin, approaching the gun where Rostov sat.
"No, it's a sprain."
"Then what's this blood on the gun carriage?" asked Tushin.
"It was the officer, sir, who stained it," answered the artilleryman, wiping the blood away with his sleeve, as if apologizing for the state of his gun.

They could barely get the guns up the hill with the infantry's help, and when they reached the village of Gruntersdorf, they stopped. It had grown so dark that you couldn't tell uniforms apart from ten paces away, and the firing had begun to die down. Suddenly, close by on the right, shouting and shooting broke out again. Flashes of gunfire gleamed in the darkness. This was the last French attack, and it was met by soldiers who had taken shelter in the village houses. They all rushed out of the village again, but Tushin's guns couldn't move, and the artillerymen, Tushin, and the cadet exchanged silent glances as they waited for their fate. The firing died down and soldiers came streaming out of a side street, talking excitedly.
"You okay, Petrov?" asked one.
"We really let them have it! They won't try again now," said another.
"You couldn't see a thing. They were shooting at their own men! Total darkness, brother! Got anything to drink?"
The French had been driven back for the last time. And once again, in the total darkness, Tushin's guns moved forward, surrounded by the humming infantry like a frame around a picture.

In the darkness, it felt as though a gloomy, invisible river was flowing in one direction, humming with whispers and talk and the sound of hooves and wheels. Above the general rumble, the groans and voices of the wounded could be heard more clearly than anything else in the darkness of the night. Their groans seemed to merge with the darkness itself. After a while, the moving mass grew agitated. Someone rode past on a white horse with his staff and said something as he passed. "What did he say? Where are we going now? Are we stopping? Did he thank us?" came eager questions from all sides. The whole mass began pressing closer together, and word spread that they had been ordered to halt—evidently those in front had stopped. Everyone stayed where they were in the middle of the muddy road.

Fires were lit and the conversations grew louder. Captain Tushin, after giving orders to his company, sent a soldier to find a field hospital or a doctor for the cadet, and sat down by a bonfire the soldiers had built on the road. Rostov also dragged himself to the fire. From the pain, cold, and dampness, feverish shivers shook his whole body. Drowsiness was overpowering him, but he stayed awake because of the agonizing pain in his arm, for which he could find no comfortable position. He kept closing his eyes and then looking at the fire again, which seemed blindingly red, and at the small, round-shouldered figure of Tushin sitting cross-legged like a Turk beside him. Tushin's large, kind, intelligent eyes were fixed on Rostov with sympathy and compassion. Rostov could see that Tushin wanted with his whole heart to help but couldn't.

From all sides came the footsteps and voices of infantry walking, driving past, and settling in all around. The sounds of voices, tramping feet, horses' hooves in the mud, and crackling fires near and far merged into one trembling rumble.

It was no longer a dark, unseen river flowing through the gloom, but a dark sea gradually settling after a storm. Rostov looked and listened listlessly to what was happening around him. An infantryman came to the fire, squatted down, held his hands to the flames, and turned away.
"You don't mind, sir?" he asked Tushin. "I've lost my company, sir. I don't know where... what rotten luck!"

Along with the soldier, an infantry officer with a bandaged cheek came up to the fire and asked Tushin to move the guns slightly to let a wagon through. After he left, two soldiers rushed up to the campfire, fighting desperately over a boot they had both grabbed.
"You found it? Yeah right! Real clever!" one of them shouted hoarsely.
Then a thin, pale soldier with a bloody bandage around his neck came up and angrily asked the artillerymen for water.
"Do I have to die like a dog?" he said.
Tushin told them to give the man some water. Then a cheerful soldier ran up, asking for a bit of fire for the infantry.
"A nice little torch for the infantry! Good luck, fellow countrymen. Thanks for the fire—we'll pay it back with interest," he said, carrying a glowing stick off into the darkness.
Next came four soldiers carrying something heavy on a cloak, and they passed by the fire. One of them stumbled.
"Who the hell put those logs on the road?" he snarled.
"He's dead—why carry him?" said another.
"Shut up!"
And they disappeared into the darkness with their burden.
"Still hurting?" Tushin asked Rostov in a whisper.
"Yes."
"Sir, the general wants you. He's in the hut over there," said a gunner, coming up to Tushin.
"Coming, friend."
Tushin got up, buttoned his greatcoat, straightened it, and walked away from the fire.

Not far from the artillery campfire, in a hut that had been prepared for him, Prince Bagration sat at dinner, talking with several commanding officers who had gathered at his quarters. The little old man with half-closed eyes was there, greedily gnawing a mutton bone. The general who had served blamelessly for twenty-two years was there too, flushed from a glass of vodka and dinner. So was the staff officer with the signet ring, and Zherkov, glancing uneasily at everyone, and Prince Andrew, pale, with tight lips and feverishly bright eyes.

In a corner of the hut stood a captured French standard, and the accountant with the innocent face was fingering its fabric, shaking his head in confusion—perhaps because the banner genuinely interested him, or perhaps because it was hard for him, hungry as he was, to watch a dinner where there was no place for him. In the next hut was a French colonel who had been captured by their dragoons. Officers were crowding in to look at him. Prince Bagration was thanking the individual commanders and asking about the details of the battle and their losses. The general whose regiment had been inspected at Braunau was telling the prince that as soon as the fighting began, he had pulled back from the woods, gathered the men who were cutting timber, let the French pass, and then made a bayonet charge with two battalions that broke up the French troops.

"When I saw, your excellency, that their first battalion was falling apart, I stopped on the road and thought: 'I'll let them come closer and then hit them with the full firepower of the battalion'—and that's exactly what I did."

The general had wanted so badly to do this and was so sorry he hadn't managed to that he had come to believe it had actually happened. Perhaps it really had? Who could sort out what did or didn't happen in all that chaos?

"By the way, your excellency, I should mention," he continued, remembering Dolokhov's conversation with Kutuzov and his last encounter with the soldier, "that Private Dolokhov, who was demoted to the ranks, captured a French officer right in front of me and showed exceptional courage."

"I saw the Pavlograd hussars attack there, your excellency," Zherkov chimed in, looking around nervously. He hadn't actually seen the hussars all day but had heard about them from an infantry officer. "They broke through two enemy formations, your excellency."

Several people smiled at Zherkov's words, expecting one of his usual jokes, but when they realized what he said reflected well on their forces and the day's work, they put on serious expressions—even though many of them knew it was a complete fabrication. Prince Bagration turned to the old colonel:

"Gentlemen, I thank you all. Every branch has performed heroically—infantry, cavalry, and artillery. But how were two guns left behind in the center?" he asked, looking around for someone. (Prince Bagration didn't ask about the guns on the left flank; he already knew they had all been abandoned at the very start of the battle.) "I believe I sent you?" he added, turning to the staff officer on duty.
"One was damaged," the staff officer answered, "and the other I can't explain. I was there the whole time, giving orders, and had only just left... It's true it was intense there," he added modestly.
Someone mentioned that Captain Tushin was camped nearby and had already been sent for.
"Oh, but you were there?" said Prince Bagration, turning to Prince Andrew.
"Of course—we just barely missed each other," said the staff officer with a smile to Bolkonsky.
"I didn't have the pleasure of seeing you," said Prince Andrew, coldly and sharply.

Everyone fell silent. Tushin appeared in the doorway and made his way timidly past the generals in the crowded hut, embarrassed as he always was around his superiors. He didn't notice the standard's staff and tripped over it. Several people laughed.
"How was it that a gun was abandoned?" asked Bagration, frowning—not so much at the captain as at those who were laughing, especially Zherkov, who laughed loudest.

Only now, faced with the stern authorities, did the full horror of his guilt and the disgrace of having lost two guns while still being alive hit Tushin. He had been so caught up in the action that he hadn't thought about it until this moment. The officers' laughter confused him even more. He stood before Bagration with his lower jaw trembling, barely able to stammer: "I don't know... your excellency... I had no men... your excellency."
"You could have taken some from the covering troops."

Tushin didn't say that there had been no covering troops, even though that was completely true. He was afraid of getting another officer in trouble and silently fixed his eyes on Bagration, like a schoolboy who has made a mistake staring at the examiner.

The silence lasted for some time. Prince Bagration, apparently not wanting to be harsh, couldn't find anything to say. The others didn't dare to step in. Prince Andrew looked at Tushin from under his brows, his fingers twitching nervously.

"Your excellency!" Prince Andrew broke the silence with his sharp voice. "You sent me to Captain Tushin's battery. I went there and found two-thirds of the men and horses killed or wounded, two guns destroyed, and no support whatsoever."
Prince Bagration and Tushin both stared intently at Bolkonsky, who spoke with barely controlled emotion.

"And, if your excellency will allow me to say so," he continued, "we owe today's success mainly to the action of that battery and the heroic endurance of Captain Tushin and his men." Without waiting for a reply, Prince Andrew stood up and left the table.

Prince Bagration looked at Tushin. He was clearly reluctant to distrust Bolkonsky's passionate opinion, yet not quite able to fully accept it either. He nodded and told Tushin he could go. Prince Andrew walked out with him.
"Thank you—you saved me, my friend!" said Tushin.
Prince Andrew glanced at him but said nothing and walked away. He felt sad and depressed. It was all so strange, so unlike what he had hoped for.

"Who are they? Why are they here? What do they want? And when will all this end?" thought Rostov, watching the shifting shadows before him. The pain in his arm grew worse and worse. Unstoppable drowsiness overcame him. Red rings danced before his eyes, and the impression of those voices and faces and a feeling of loneliness merged with the physical pain. It was they, these soldiers—wounded and unwounded—who were crushing, pressing down, and twisting the muscles and burning the flesh of his sprained arm and shoulder. To escape them, he closed his eyes.

For a moment he dozed off, but in that brief interval countless things appeared to him in a dream: his mother and her large white hand, Sonya's thin little shoulders, Natasha's eyes and laughter, Denisov with his voice and mustache, and Telyanin and that whole affair with Telyanin and Bogdanich. That affair was the same thing as this soldier with the harsh voice, and it was that affair and this soldier that kept agonizingly, relentlessly pulling and pressing his arm, always dragging it in one direction. He tried to get away from them, but they wouldn't let his shoulder move even a hair's breadth. It wouldn't hurt—it would be fine—if only they would stop pulling it, but he couldn't get rid of them.

He opened his eyes and looked up. The black canopy of night hung less than a yard above the glow of the coals. Flakes of falling snow drifted through the light. Tushin hadn't come back, the doctor hadn't come. He was alone now, except for a soldier sitting naked on the other side of the fire, warming his thin yellow body.
"Nobody wants me!" thought Rostov. "There is no one to help me or feel sorry for me. Yet I was once at home, strong, happy, and loved." He sighed and, as he did, groaned involuntarily.
"Hey, something hurting you?" asked the soldier, shaking out his shirt over the fire. Without waiting for an answer, he grunted and added: "What a lot of men got mangled today—terrible!"

Rostov wasn't listening. He watched the snowflakes fluttering above the fire and remembered a Russian winter at his warm, bright home, his fluffy fur coat, his sleigh gliding quickly along, his healthy body, and all the love and care of his family. "Why did I come here?" he wondered.
The next day the French did not attack again, and the remnants of Bagration's force rejoined Kutuzov's army.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Prince Vasili was not a man who carefully planned things out. Even less did he deliberately scheme to hurt anyone for his own benefit. He was simply a man of the world who had learned how to get ahead, and getting ahead had become second nature to him. Plans and strategies that he never quite acknowledged to himself, but that made up the entire interest of his life, were constantly forming in his mind, sparked by the people and situations he encountered. He didn't have just one or two such plans going at once, but dozens—some barely taking shape, some nearing completion, and some already falling apart. He never said to himself, for instance, 'This man has influence, so I need to win his trust and use him to get a special appointment.' Nor did he think, 'Pierre is rich, so I should get him to marry my daughter and lend me forty thousand rubles.' But whenever he met someone powerful, his instincts immediately told him that person could be useful, and without any forethought, Prince Vasili would seize the first opportunity to gain his confidence, flatter him, become close to him, and eventually make his request.

He had Pierre right there in Moscow, so he arranged an appointment for him as Gentleman of the Bedchamber—which at the time carried the status of Councilor of State—and insisted the young man come with him to Petersburg and stay at his house. With what looked like absent-mindedness, yet with unwavering confidence that he was doing the right thing, Prince Vasili did everything to get Pierre to marry his daughter. If he had actually planned it all out, he couldn't have been so natural or shown such relaxed familiarity with people both above and below him in social standing. Something always drew him toward those richer and more powerful than himself, and he had a rare talent for choosing exactly the right moment to use people.

Pierre, who had unexpectedly become Count Bezukhov and a rich man, felt so overwhelmed after his recent loneliness and freedom that he could only be by himself in bed. He had to sign papers, visit government offices whose purpose he didn't understand, consult his head steward, inspect his estate near Moscow, and receive a stream of people who had previously ignored his existence but would now have been offended if he hadn't seen them. All of these people—businessmen, relatives, acquaintances—treated the young heir with the greatest friendliness and flattery. They were all obviously convinced of Pierre's fine qualities. He kept hearing things like: 'With your remarkable kindness,' or 'With your excellent heart,' 'You are such an honorable man, Count,' or 'If only he were as clever as you.' He began to genuinely believe in his own exceptional kindness and extraordinary intelligence, especially since, deep down, he had always felt he really was kind and intelligent. Even people who had been unfriendly before now became warm and affectionate. The stern eldest princess, with her long waist and doll-like plastered-down hair, had come to Pierre's room after the funeral. With lowered eyes and frequent blushes, she told him she was sorry about their past disagreements and now felt she had no right to ask anything—only permission, after the blow she had suffered, to stay a few more weeks in the house she loved so much and where she had sacrificed so much. She couldn't hold back her tears. Moved by this transformation in the stiff princess, Pierre took her hand and begged her forgiveness, without knowing what for. From that day on, the eldest princess completely changed toward Pierre and even began knitting him a striped scarf.
"Do this for me, my dear—after all, she had to put up with a great deal from the deceased," said Prince Vasili, handing Pierre a document to sign for the princess's benefit.

Prince Vasili had decided it was necessary to throw this bone—a thirty-thousand-ruble payment—to the poor princess, so it wouldn't occur to her to talk about his role in the affair of the inlaid portfolio. Pierre signed the document, and after that the princess became even kinder. The younger sisters also grew affectionate toward him, especially the youngest, the pretty one with the mole, who often made him feel flustered with her smiles and her own blushing whenever they met.

It seemed so natural to Pierre that everyone liked him, and it would have seemed so strange if anyone hadn't, that he couldn't help believing in the sincerity of those around him. Besides, he was always busy and felt in a constant state of mild, cheerful excitement. He felt like the center of some important movement—that people were always expecting something of him, that if he didn't deliver he would disappoint many people, but if he just did this and that, everything would be fine. And so he did what was asked of him, but that happy outcome always remained somewhere in the future.

More than anyone, Prince Vasili took charge of Pierre's affairs and of Pierre himself during those early days. From the death of Count Bezukhov, he never let go of the young man. He had the manner of someone burdened with business, weary and suffering, who nevertheless wouldn't abandon this helpless youth—after all, the son of his old friend and the owner of such enormous wealth—to the whims of fate and the schemes of villains. During his few days in Moscow after Count Bezukhov's death, he would summon Pierre or visit him, telling him what needed to be done in a tired, confident tone, as if adding each time: 'You know I'm overwhelmed with work and it's purely out of kindness that I bother with you, and you know perfectly well that what I'm proposing is the only sensible option.'

"Well, my dear fellow, tomorrow we're off at last," said Prince Vasili one day, closing his eyes and touching Pierre's elbow, speaking as if they had agreed on this long ago and it couldn't be changed. "We leave tomorrow and I'm giving you a place in my carriage. I'm very glad. All our important business here is settled, and I should have left ages ago. Here's something I received from the chancellor. I asked him on your behalf, and you've been accepted into the diplomatic corps and made a Gentleman of the Bedchamber. A diplomatic career now lies open before you."

Despite the weary confidence with which these words were delivered, Pierre, who had been thinking about his future for a long time, wanted to say something. But Prince Vasili cut him off in that special deep, cooing tone he used in extreme cases when special persuasion was needed—a tone that made interruption impossible.

"But my dear, I did this for my own sake, to satisfy my conscience, and there's nothing to thank me for. No one has ever complained about being loved too much. Besides, you're free—you could drop the whole thing tomorrow. But you'll see everything for yourself when you get to Petersburg. It's time you got away from these terrible memories." Prince Vasili sighed. "Yes, yes, my boy. And my valet can ride in your carriage. Oh, I nearly forgot," he added. "You know, my dear, your father and I had some financial matters between us, so I've collected what was due from the Ryazan estate and I'll keep it. You won't be needing it. We'll sort out the accounts later."
By 'what was due from the Ryazan estate,' Prince Vasili meant several thousand rubles in rent payments from Pierre's peasants, which the prince had pocketed for himself.

In Petersburg, as in Moscow, Pierre found the same atmosphere of warmth and friendliness. He couldn't refuse the position—or rather the rank, since he did nothing—that Prince Vasili had arranged for him. Social obligations, invitations, and engagements were so numerous that here, even more than in Moscow, he felt a sense of bewilderment, bustle, and constant expectation of something good that was always just ahead but never quite arrived.

Many of his former bachelor friends were no longer in Petersburg. The Guards had gone to the front. Dolokhov had been demoted to the ranks. Anatole was somewhere in the provinces with the army. Prince Andrew was abroad. So Pierre had no chance to spend his evenings the way he used to, or to have intimate, heart-to-heart conversations with an older friend he respected. His entire time was consumed by dinners and balls, mostly spent at Prince Vasili's house in the company of the stout princess, his wife, and their beautiful daughter Hélène.
Like everyone else, Anna Pavlovna Scherer showed Pierre the change in attitude that society had adopted toward him.

Before, in Anna Pavlovna's presence, Pierre had always felt that everything he said was out of place, tactless, and awkward—that remarks which seemed clever in his head sounded stupid the moment he spoke them, while Hippolyte's dumbest comments somehow came out witty and clever. Now everything Pierre said was charming. Even if Anna Pavlovna didn't say so directly, he could tell she wanted to and only held back out of respect for his modesty.
In the early winter of 1805-06, Pierre received one of Anna Pavlovna's usual pink invitations, with a note added: 'You will find the beautiful Hélène here, whom it is always a delight to see.'

When he read that line, Pierre felt for the first time that some connection that others could see had formed between him and Hélène. The thought both alarmed him—as if some obligation were being placed on him that he couldn't fulfill—and pleased him as an intriguing possibility.

Anna Pavlovna's party was like the previous one, except this time the novelty she offered her guests was not Mortemart but a diplomat fresh from Berlin, bringing the latest details about Emperor Alexander's visit to Potsdam and how the two great friends had pledged an unbreakable alliance to uphold justice against the enemy of mankind. Anna Pavlovna greeted Pierre with a touch of sadness, clearly referring to the young man's recent loss of his father (everyone felt obligated to remind Pierre how devastated he must be by the death of a father he had barely known), and her sadness matched the grand melancholy she displayed when mentioning Her Most August Majesty the Empress. Pierre felt flattered. Anna Pavlovna arranged the groups in her drawing room with her usual skill. The larger group, which included Prince Vasili and the generals, had the diplomat's attention. Another group gathered around the tea table. Pierre wanted to join the first, but Anna Pavlovna—in the excited state of a battlefield commander with a thousand brilliant ideas and not enough time to execute them all—spotted Pierre, touched his sleeve with her finger, and said:

"Wait, I have something in mind for you this evening." She glanced at Hélène and smiled. "My dear Hélène, be kind to my poor aunt who adores you. Go keep her company for ten minutes. And so it won't be too boring, here is the dear count, who I'm sure won't refuse to go with you."
The beauty went to the aunt, but Anna Pavlovna held Pierre back, looking as if she had some final essential instructions.

"Isn't she magnificent?" she said to Pierre, pointing to the stately beauty gliding away. "And such poise! For such a young woman, such perfect manners! It comes from the heart. The man who wins her will be lucky indeed. With her, even the most ordinary man would have a brilliant position in society. Don't you agree? I just wanted to hear your opinion." And Anna Pavlovna let Pierre go.
Pierre sincerely agreed about Hélène's perfect manners. Whenever he thought of Hélène, it was only of her beauty and her remarkable ability to appear silently dignified in any social setting.

The old aunt received the two young people in her corner but seemed more interested in hiding her adoration for Hélène and showing her fear of Anna Pavlovna. She looked at her niece as if asking what to do with these visitors. As she left them, Anna Pavlovna touched Pierre's sleeve again: "I hope you won't say it's boring at my house again." She glanced at Hélène.

Hélène smiled with a look that said she couldn't imagine anyone seeing her without being enchanted. The aunt coughed, swallowed, and told Hélène in French how pleased she was to see her, then turned to Pierre with the same greeting and the same look. In the middle of a halting, dull conversation, Hélène turned to Pierre with the beautiful, radiant smile she gave everyone. Pierre was so used to that smile, and it meant so little to him, that he paid no attention. The aunt was talking about a collection of snuffboxes that had belonged to Pierre's father, Count Bezukhov, and showed them her own. Princess Hélène asked to see the portrait of the aunt's husband on the lid.
"That's probably by Vinesse," said Pierre, naming a famous miniaturist, and he leaned over the table to take the snuffbox while trying to hear the conversation at the other table.

He half stood up, meaning to walk around, but the aunt handed him the snuffbox across Hélène's back. Hélène leaned forward to make room and looked back with a smile. She was wearing, as always at evening parties, a dress cut very low at the front and back, in the fashion of the time. Her bust, which had always seemed like marble to Pierre, was so close that his nearsighted eyes couldn't help noticing the living warmth of her neck and shoulders, so near his lips that he would only have had to bend his head slightly to touch them. He felt the warmth of her body, smelled her perfume, and heard the creaking of her corset as she moved. He no longer saw her marble beauty as a complete whole unified with her dress—instead, he saw all the charm of her body barely concealed by her clothing. And once he had seen this, he couldn't unsee it, just as you can't restore an illusion you've seen through.

"So you've never noticed before how beautiful I am?" Hélène seemed to say. "You hadn't realized I'm a woman? Yes, I am a woman who could belong to anyone—to you too," said her glance. And at that moment Pierre felt that Hélène not only could but must be his wife, and that it couldn't be any other way.

He knew this as surely as if he had been standing at the altar with her. How and when it would happen he didn't know; he didn't even know if it would be a good thing (he even felt, for some reason he couldn't explain, that it would be a bad thing), but he knew it would happen.

Pierre dropped his eyes, then raised them again, trying to see her once more as a distant beauty far removed from him—the way he had seen her every day until then. But he could no longer do it. He couldn't, just as a man who has mistaken a tuft of steppe grass for a tree through the mist can never see it as a tree again once he recognizes what it is. She was terribly close. She already had power over him. Between them there was no barrier except the barrier of his own will.
"Well, I'll leave you in your little corner," came Anna Pavlovna's voice. "I can see you're doing just fine there."
And Pierre, anxiously trying to remember if he'd done anything wrong, looked around with a blush. It seemed to him that everyone knew what had happened to him, just as he knew it himself.
A little later, when he joined the larger group, Anna Pavlovna said to him: "I hear you're renovating your Petersburg house?"
This was true. The architect had told him it was necessary, and Pierre, without knowing why, was having his enormous Petersburg mansion redone.

"That's a good thing, but don't move out of Prince Vasili's. It's good to have a friend like the prince," she said, smiling at Prince Vasili. "I know a thing or two about that, don't I? And you're still so young. You need advice. Don't be angry with me for exercising an old woman's privilege."

She paused, as women always do after mentioning their age. "If you marry, that will be a different matter," she continued, her glance linking them both. Pierre didn't look at Hélène and she didn't look at him. But she was just as terrifyingly close. He mumbled something and blushed.

When he got home, he couldn't sleep for a long time, thinking about what had happened. What had happened? Nothing. He had simply realized that the woman he had known since childhood—about whom he would say casually when her beauty was mentioned, 'Yes, she's good-looking'—he had realized that this woman could be his.

"But she's stupid. I've said so myself," he thought. "There's something wrong, something ugly, about the feeling she stirs in me. I've been told that her brother Anatole was in love with her and she with him, that there was a real scandal, and that's why he was sent away. Hippolyte is her brother... Prince Vasili is her father... This is wrong..." he reflected. But even as he thought this—and the thought was still incomplete—he caught himself smiling and realized a completely different train of thought had taken over. While thinking about her flaws, he was simultaneously dreaming about how she would be his wife, how she would love him and become entirely different, and how everything he had thought and heard about her might be false. And once again he saw her, not as Prince Vasili's daughter, but her whole body only veiled by its gray dress. "But no! Why didn't this occur to me before?" And again he told himself it was impossible, that there would be something unnatural, something dishonorable about this marriage. He remembered her past words and looks and the words and looks of those who had seen them together. He recalled Anna Pavlovna's comments about his house, remembered a thousand similar hints from Prince Vasili and others, and was seized with terror that he had somehow already bound himself to do something clearly wrong that he ought not to do. But even as he was convincing himself of this, in another part of his mind her image rose in all its feminine beauty.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Shortly after nine that evening, Weyrother arrived at Kutuzov's quarters with his plans for the council of war. All the column commanders had been summoned, and all except Prince Bagration, who declined to attend, were there at the appointed time.

Weyrother, who was fully in charge of the planned battle, presented a sharp contrast in his eagerness and energy to the dissatisfied and drowsy Kutuzov, who reluctantly played the role of chairman. Weyrother was clearly aware he was driving a movement that had already become unstoppable. He was like a horse harnessed to a heavy cart running downhill — whether he was pulling it or being pushed by it, he couldn't tell, but he rushed forward at breakneck speed with no time to think about where this was all heading. He had been to the enemy's picket line twice that evening to scout in person, twice to the Russian and Austrian Emperors to report and explain, and to his own headquarters where he had dictated the battle plan in German. Now, thoroughly exhausted, he arrived at Kutuzov's.

He was so preoccupied that he forgot even basic courtesy toward the commander in chief. He interrupted him, spoke rapidly and indistinctly without looking at the person he was addressing, and ignored questions put to him. He was spattered with mud and had a harried, exhausted, distracted look about him, though at the same time he was arrogant and self-assured.

Kutuzov was occupying a modest nobleman's manor near Ostralitz. In the large drawing room that had become the commander in chief's office, Kutuzov himself, Weyrother, and the other council members had gathered. They were drinking tea and waiting only for Prince Bagration to begin. Finally Bagration's orderly arrived with the news that the prince could not attend. Prince Andrew came in to report this to the commander in chief and, having previously received Kutuzov's permission to attend the council, remained in the room.
"Since Prince Bagration isn't coming, we may as well begin," said Weyrother, hurriedly rising and going to the table where an enormous map of the area around Brunn was spread out.

Kutuzov, his uniform unbuttoned so that his thick neck bulged over his collar as though trying to escape, sat almost asleep in a low chair, his pudgy old hands resting symmetrically on the armrests. At the sound of Weyrother's voice, he opened one eye with effort.
"Yes, yes, go ahead. It's already late," he said, and nodding his head he let it droop and closed his eye again.

If at first the council members thought Kutuzov was only pretending to sleep, the sounds that soon came from his nose proved that the commander in chief was absorbed by something far more pressing than any desire to show his contempt for the battle plan or anything else — he was satisfying the irresistible human need for sleep. He was genuinely asleep. Weyrother, with the manner of a man too busy to waste a single moment, glanced at Kutuzov, confirmed he was asleep, picked up a paper, and in a loud, monotonous voice began reading out the battle plan, starting with its title:
"Dispositions for an attack on the enemy position behind Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz, November 30, 1805."
The dispositions were extremely complicated and difficult to follow. They began:

"Since the enemy's left wing rests on wooded hills and his right extends along Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz behind the ponds there, while we on the other hand far outflank his right with our left wing, it is advantageous to attack the enemy's right wing, especially if we occupy the villages of Sokolnitz and Kobelnitz, whereby we can both strike his flank and pursue him across the plain between Schlappanitz and the Thuerassa forest, avoiding the defiles of Schlappanitz and Bellowitz that cover the enemy's front. To this end it is necessary that... The first column marches... The second column marches... The third column marches..." and so on, Weyrother read.

The generals appeared to listen reluctantly to the complicated orders. The tall, fair-haired General Buxhowden stood leaning against the wall, his eyes fixed on a burning candle, seeming not to listen — or even wanting to be thought to listen. Directly opposite Weyrother sat the ruddy-faced Miloradovich, holding a military pose with his elbows out, hands on his knees, and shoulders raised, his glistening wide eyes fixed on Weyrother and his mustache twisted upward. He remained stubbornly silent, staring at Weyrother's face, and only looked away when the Austrian chief of staff finished reading. Then Miloradovich glanced around meaningfully at the other generals, though it was impossible to tell from that look whether he agreed or disagreed, was satisfied or not. Beside Weyrother sat Count Langeron, who wore the subtle smile that never left his typically southern French face throughout the entire reading, as he gazed at his slender fingers rapidly spinning a gold snuffbox adorned with a portrait. Midway through one of the longest sentences, he stopped spinning the snuffbox, raised his head, and with a thin-lipped smile of hostile politeness tried to interrupt Weyrother to make a point. But the Austrian general, still reading, frowned angrily and jerked his elbows, as if to say: "You can share your views later — for now, kindly look at the map and listen." Langeron raised his eyebrows in confusion, glanced at Miloradovich as if seeking support, but meeting the latter's impressive yet meaningless gaze, he dropped his eyes sadly and went back to spinning his snuffbox.
"A geography lesson!" he muttered, seemingly to himself but loud enough for everyone to hear.

Przhebyshevsky, with respectful but dignified politeness, cupped his hand to his ear toward Weyrother, with the air of a man deeply absorbed in concentration. Dokhturov, a small man sitting opposite Weyrother, leaned over the spread-out map with a conscientious and modest expression, earnestly studying the battle plan and the unfamiliar terrain. He asked Weyrother several times to repeat words he hadn't caught clearly and the difficult names of villages. Weyrother obliged, and Dokhturov noted them down.

When the reading — which lasted more than an hour — was over, Langeron set down his snuffbox again and, without looking at Weyrother or anyone in particular, began explaining how difficult it would be to carry out such a plan when the enemy's position was only assumed and not actually known, since the enemy might well be on the move. Langeron's objections were valid, but it was clear that his main purpose was to show General Weyrother — who had read his plan with the self-assurance of a teacher lecturing schoolchildren — that he was not dealing with fools, but with men who could teach him a thing or two about military affairs.

When the monotonous drone of Weyrother's voice stopped, Kutuzov opened his eye the way a miller wakes up when the soothing hum of the mill wheel suddenly stops. He listened to Langeron's remarks as if to say, "So you're still going on with this nonsense!" then quickly closed his eye again and let his head sink even lower.

Langeron, trying as sharply as possible to wound Weyrother's pride as the plan's author, argued that Bonaparte might easily attack rather than be attacked, which would make the entire plan worthless. Weyrother met every objection with a firm, contemptuous smile, clearly having prepared responses to any possible criticism.
"If he could have attacked us, he would have done so today," he said.
"So you think he's powerless?" said Langeron.
"He has forty thousand men at most," Weyrother replied, with the smile of a doctor whose elderly patient is trying to tell him how to treat the case.
"In that case he's practically inviting his own destruction by waiting for our attack," said Langeron with a subtly mocking smile, again glancing around at Miloradovich for support.
But Miloradovich was obviously thinking about anything other than what the generals were arguing about.
"Well!" he said. "Tomorrow we'll see it all on the battlefield."

Weyrother again gave that smile that seemed to say he found it both strange and absurd to face objections from Russian generals and to have to prove things he had already convinced not just himself of, but the Emperors as well.

"The enemy has put out his fires and there's a constant noise coming from his camp," he said. "What does that mean? Either he's retreating — which is the only thing we need to worry about — or he's changing position." He smiled knowingly. "But even if he also takes up a position in the Thuerassa, he merely saves us a great deal of trouble, and all our plans down to the smallest detail remain the same."
"How is that..." Prince Andrew began. He had been waiting a long time for a chance to voice his doubts.
But at that moment Kutuzov woke up, coughed heavily, and looked around at the generals.

"Gentlemen, the plans for tomorrow — or rather for today, since it is past midnight — can no longer be changed," he said. "You have heard them, and we shall all do our duty. But before a battle, there is nothing more important..." He paused. "...than a good night's sleep."
He moved as if to stand. The generals bowed and withdrew. It was past midnight. Prince Andrew went out.

The council of war, at which Prince Andrew had not managed to express the opinion he'd hoped to share, left him with a vague, uneasy feeling. Whether Dolgorukov and Weyrother were right, or Kutuzov, Langeron, and the others who opposed the plan of attack — he couldn't tell. "But was it really impossible for Kutuzov to speak plainly to the Emperor? Is it possible that because of court politics and personal considerations, tens of thousands of lives — and my life, my life," he thought, "must be put at risk?"

"Yes, it's very likely that I'll be killed tomorrow," he thought. And suddenly, at this thought of death, a whole series of distant, deeply personal memories rose in his mind: he remembered his last farewell to his father and his wife; he remembered the early days when he first loved her. He thought about her pregnancy and felt sorry for her, and for himself, and in this nervously emotional, tender mood he walked out of the cabin where he was quartered with Nesvitsky and began pacing back and forth outside it.

The night was foggy, and through the mist the moonlight shimmered eerily. "Yes, tomorrow, tomorrow!" he thought. "Tomorrow everything may be over for me! All these memories will mean nothing — none of them will matter anymore. Tomorrow perhaps — almost certainly — I have a feeling that for the first time I'll have a chance to show everything I'm capable of." And in his imagination the battle unfolded: the defeat, the fighting concentrated at one crucial point, the hesitation of all the commanders. And then that glorious moment — that Toulon he had waited for so long — finally arrives. He states his views firmly and clearly to Kutuzov, to Weyrother, and to the Emperors. Everyone is struck by the brilliance of his analysis, but no one dares to carry it out, so he takes a regiment, a division — on the condition that no one interferes with his command — leads his division to the decisive point, and wins the victory single-handedly. "But death and suffering?" suggested another voice. Prince Andrew, however, did not answer that voice and continued dreaming of his triumphs. The plans for the next battle are drawn up by him alone. Officially he is still just an adjutant on Kutuzov's staff, but he does everything himself. The next battle is won by him alone. Kutuzov is removed, and he is appointed... "And then what?" asked the other voice. "If before that you're not wounded ten times over, or killed, or betrayed — then what?" "Well then," Prince Andrew answered himself, "I don't know what will happen and don't want to know, and can't know. But if I want this — want glory, want to be known, want to be loved — it's not my fault that I want it and want nothing else and live for nothing else. Yes, for that alone! I will never tell anyone this, but oh God! What am I supposed to do if I love nothing but glory and the esteem of others? Death, wounds, the loss of family — none of it frightens me. And dear as so many people are to me — my father, my sister, my wife — the people closest to me — yet terrible and unnatural as it seems, I would give them all up in an instant for one moment of glory, of triumph, of love from people I don't know and never will know — for the love of these men here," he thought, listening to voices in Kutuzov's courtyard. It was the orderlies packing up; one voice, probably a coachman's, was teasing Kutuzov's old cook, whom Prince Andrew knew — a man called Tit. "Tit, hey, Tit!" he was saying.
"What?" the old man replied.
"Go on, Tit, go thresh a bit!" said the joker.
"Oh, go to hell!" called out a voice, drowned by the laughter of the orderlies and servants.
"All the same, I love and value nothing but victory over them all — this mysterious power and glory that hovers here above me in the mist!"

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Early in 1806, Nicholas Rostov returned home on leave. Denisov was heading to Voronezh, and Rostov convinced him to travel together as far as Moscow and stay with him there. At the last post station before Moscow, Denisov had drunk three bottles of wine with a fellow officer and, despite the jolting ride over the rutted, snow-covered road, slept the entire way, lying at the bottom of the sleigh beside Rostov, who grew more and more impatient as they neared the city.

"How much farther? How much longer? These unbearable streets, shops, bakery signs, street lamps, and sleighs!" Rostov thought, after their travel permits had been checked at the city gate and they had entered Moscow.
"Denisov! We're here! He's asleep," he added, leaning his whole body forward as if that might somehow make the sleigh go faster.
Denisov didn't answer.

"There's the corner where the cabman Zakhar has his stand — and there's Zakhar himself, with the same old horse! And there's the little shop where we used to buy gingerbread! Can't you go faster? Come on!"
"Which house?" asked the driver.
"That one, right at the end, the big one. Can't you see? That's our house," said Rostov. "Of course it's our house! Denisov, Denisov! We're almost there!"
Denisov lifted his head, coughed, and said nothing.
"Dmitri," said Rostov to his servant on the box, "those lights are in our house, aren't they?"
"Yes, sir, and there's a light on in your father's study."

"So they haven't gone to bed yet! Good. And don't forget to put out my new coat," added Rostov, fingering his new mustache. "Now hurry up," he shouted to the driver. "Wake up, Vaska!" he said, turning to Denisov, whose head was nodding again. "Come on, get moving! I'll give you three rubles for vodka — just go!" Rostov shouted when the sleigh was only three houses from his door. It felt as though the horses had stopped moving entirely. At last the sleigh turned right, pulled up at an entrance, and Rostov looked up to see the old familiar cornice with its bit of chipped plaster, the porch, and the post beside the pavement. He leaped out before the sleigh had stopped and ran into the hall. The house was cold and quiet, as if it didn't care who had come to it. There was no one in the hall. "Oh God! Is everyone all right?" he thought, pausing for a moment with a sinking heart, then immediately running through the hall and up the worn, familiar staircase. The old door handle — the one that always annoyed the countess when it wasn't properly cleaned — turned as loosely as ever. A single tallow candle burned in the anteroom.

Old Mikhail was asleep on the chest. Prokofy the footman, who was so strong he could lift the back of a carriage by himself, sat braiding slippers from cloth scraps. He looked up when the door opened, and his expression of sleepy indifference instantly transformed into delighted amazement.

"Good heavens! The young count!" he cried, recognizing his young master. "Can it be? My dear boy!" And Prokofy, trembling with excitement, rushed toward the drawing room door — probably to announce him — but then changed his mind, came back, and bent down to kiss the young man's shoulder.
"Everyone well?" asked Rostov, pulling his arm away.
"Yes, thank God! Yes! They've just finished supper. Let me look at you, your excellency."
"Everything's really all right?"
"Yes, thank the Lord!"

Rostov, who had completely forgotten about Denisov and not wanting anyone to get there before him, threw off his fur coat and ran on tiptoe through the large, dark ballroom. Everything was the same: the same old card tables, the same chandelier with its dust cover. But someone had already spotted the young master, and before he reached the drawing room, something burst from a side door like a whirlwind and started hugging and kissing him. Then another creature of the same kind flew out from a second door, and a third — more hugging, more kissing, more shouts and tears of joy. He couldn't tell who was Papa, who was Natasha, and who was Petya. Everyone shouted, talked, and kissed him all at once. Only his mother was not among them, he noticed.
"I didn't know... Nicholas... My darling!..."
"Here he is... our own boy... Kolya, sweetheart... How he's changed!... Where are the candles?... Tea!..."
* Kolya is the familiar form of Nicholas.
"And me — kiss me!"
"Darling... and me!"
Sonya, Natasha, Petya, Anna Mikhaylovna, Vera, and the old count were all hugging him, while the servants — men and women alike — crowded into the room, exclaiming and gasping.
Petya clung to his legs, shouting, "And me too!"
Natasha, after pulling him down toward her and covering his face with kisses while gripping the hem of his coat, sprang away and began prancing in place like a goat, letting out a piercing shriek.
All around him were loving eyes glistening with tears of joy, and everywhere were lips seeking a kiss.

Sonya too, her face flushed pink, clung to his arm and gazed at him, radiant with happiness, eagerly waiting for the look she longed for. She was sixteen now and very pretty, especially at this moment of joyful, rapturous excitement. She stared at him without blinking, smiling and holding her breath. He gave her a grateful look but was still searching for someone. The old countess hadn't come yet. Then footsteps were heard at the door — footsteps so rapid they could hardly be his mother's.

Yet it was her, wearing a new dress he didn't recognize, made after he had left. Everyone else let go of him, and he ran to her. When they met, she fell against his chest, sobbing. She couldn't lift her face — she just pressed it against the cold braiding of his hussar jacket. Denisov, who had entered the room unnoticed, stood there and wiped his eyes at the sight.
"Vasili Denisov, your son's friend," he said, introducing himself to the count, who was looking at him questioningly.
"Welcome! Most welcome! I know, I know," said the count, kissing and embracing Denisov. "Nicholas wrote us about you... Natasha, Vera — look! Here is Denisov!"
The same happy, glowing faces turned toward Denisov's shaggy figure.

"Dear Denisov!" screamed Natasha, beside herself with joy, springing toward him, throwing her arms around him, and kissing him. This display made everyone feel a bit awkward. Denisov blushed too, but smiled, took Natasha's hand, and kissed it.
Denisov was shown to his room, and the Rostovs all gathered around Nicholas in the sitting room.

The old countess, refusing to let go of his hand and kissing it every other moment, sat beside him. The rest crowded around, watching his every movement, word, and expression, never taking their adoring eyes off him. His brother and sisters jostled for the spots closest to him and argued over who would bring him his tea, his handkerchief, his pipe.

Rostov was deeply happy in the love they showed him, but the first moment of reunion had been so perfect that now his joy seemed insufficient, and he kept expecting something more — more and still more.
The next morning, after the fatigue of their journey, the travelers slept until ten o'clock.

In the room next to their bedroom lay a jumble of sabers, satchels, sword belts, open trunks, and dirty boots. Two freshly cleaned pairs with spurs had just been set against the wall. Servants brought in pitchers and basins, hot water for shaving, and well-brushed clothes. The room smelled of men and tobacco.
"Hey, Grishka — my pipe!" came Denisov's husky voice. "Rostov, get up!"
Rostov, rubbing his eyes, which seemed glued shut, lifted his tousled head from the warm pillow.
"Is it late?"

"Late! It's nearly ten o'clock," answered Natasha's voice. A rustle of starched petticoats and the whispering and laughter of girls came from the next room. The door cracked open and there was a glimpse of something blue — ribbons, dark hair, and cheerful faces. It was Natasha, Sonya, and Petya, who had come to check if they were up yet.
"Nicholas! Get up!" Natasha's voice came again at the door.
"Coming!"

Meanwhile Petya, who had found the sabers in the outer room, seized them with a boy's natural delight at anything military. Forgetting that it wasn't proper for the girls to see men undressed, he threw open the bedroom door.
"Is this your saber?" he shouted.

The girls jumped aside. Denisov hid his hairy legs under the blanket and looked with a panicked face at his comrade for help. The door, having let Petya in, closed again. Laughter erupted from behind it.
"Nicholas! Come out in your dressing gown!" called Natasha's voice.
"Is this your saber?" asked Petya. "Or is it yours?" he added, turning to the dark-mustached Denisov with exaggerated respect.

Rostov hurriedly pulled on something for his feet, threw on his dressing gown, and came out. Natasha had put on one spurred boot and was trying to get her foot into the other. Sonya was twirling around, about to puff out her skirts like a balloon and sit down. They were both wearing identical new pale-blue dresses, and both looked fresh, rosy, and bright. Sonya ran off, but Natasha took her brother's arm and led him to the sitting room, where they started talking. They barely gave each other time to ask questions and get answers about a thousand small things that could only matter to the two of them. Natasha laughed at everything he said and everything she said — not because any of it was funny, but because she was happy and couldn't contain her joy, which came out as laughter.
"Oh, how lovely! How wonderful!" she said to everything.

Rostov felt that under the influence of the warm glow of love, the childlike smile that had not appeared on his face once since he left home now returned for the first time in eighteen months, brightening both his soul and his face.
"No, but listen," she said, "you're really a grown man now, aren't you? I'm so glad you're my brother." She touched his mustache. "I want to know what you men are like. Are you the same as us? No?"
"Why did Sonya run away?" asked Rostov.
"Oh, that's a whole long story! How are you going to talk to her — formally or informally?"
"However it happens," said Rostov.
"No, use the formal 'you,' please! I'll tell you all about it another time. Actually, I'll tell you now. You know Sonya is my dearest friend. Such a close friend that I burned my arm for her. Look!"
She pushed up her muslin sleeve and showed him a red scar on her long, slender arm, high above the elbow — a spot normally covered even by a ball gown.
"I burned this to prove my love for her. I just heated a ruler over a candle and pressed it right there!"

Sitting on the sofa with the little cushions on its arms, in what had been his old schoolroom, looking into Natasha's wildly bright eyes, Rostov re-entered that world of home and childhood that meant nothing to anyone else but gave him some of the greatest joys of his life. Burning one's arm with a ruler to prove love didn't seem senseless to him — he understood it and wasn't surprised by it at all.
"And that's all?" he asked.

"We're such friends, such close friends! All that ruler business was just silliness, but we're friends forever. When she loves someone, she does it for life — but I'm not like that. I forget quickly."
"So what then?"
"She loves me, and she loves you the same way."
Natasha suddenly blushed.

"She says you should forget all about what happened before you left.... She says, 'I will always love him, but let him be free.' Isn't that beautiful and noble? Yes, really noble — isn't it?" asked Natasha, so seriously and passionately that it was clear she had discussed this before, with tears.
Rostov grew thoughtful.
"I never go back on my word," he said. "Besides, Sonya is so lovely that only a fool would give up such happiness."

"No, no!" cried Natasha. "She and I have already talked about this. We knew you'd say that. But it won't work, because if you say it like that — if you act like you're bound by your promise — then it seems as though she wasn't being sincere. It would make it look like you're marrying her out of obligation, and that's no good at all."

Rostov saw that they had thought this through carefully. Sonya had already struck him with her beauty the day before. Today, having caught a glimpse of her, she seemed even lovelier. She was a charming sixteen-year-old girl, obviously passionately in love with him — he didn't doubt that for a moment. Why shouldn't he love her now, and even marry her? But at the moment, there were so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him! "Yes, they've made a wise decision," he thought. "I should stay free."
"Well then, that's perfect," he said. "We'll talk about it later. Oh, how glad I am to have you!"
"So — are you still faithful to Boris?" he continued.
"Oh, what nonsense!" cried Natasha, laughing. "I don't think about him or anyone else, and I don't want any of that."
"Really! So what are you up to these days?"
"These days?" repeated Natasha, and a happy smile lit up her face. "Have you seen Duport?"
"No."
"You haven't seen Duport — the famous dancer? Well then, you won't understand. That's what I'm up to."

Curving her arms and holding out her skirts like a ballerina, Natasha backed up a few steps, spun around, performed a little jump, clicked her feet sharply together, and rose up on the very tips of her toes.
"See? I'm standing! See!" she said, but couldn't hold herself on her toes any longer. "So that's what I'm doing! I'll never marry anyone — I'm going to be a dancer. But don't tell anyone."
Rostov laughed so loudly and joyfully that Denisov in the bedroom felt a pang of envy, and Natasha couldn't help joining in.
"Don't you think it's wonderful?" she kept repeating.
"Wonderful! And so you don't want to marry Boris anymore?"
Natasha flared up. "I don't want to marry anyone. And I'll tell him so myself when I see him!"
"Goodness!" said Rostov.
"But that's all silly," Natasha chattered on. "Is Denisov nice?" she asked.
"Very nice."
"Well then — goodbye. Go get dressed. Is he very scary, Denisov?"
"Why scary?" asked Nicholas. "No, Vaska is a wonderful fellow."
"You call him Vaska? That's funny! Is he really nice?"
"Very."
"All right then, hurry up. We'll all have breakfast together."

And Natasha rose and tiptoed out of the room like a ballerina, but with the kind of smile that only happy fifteen-year-old girls can manage. When Rostov met Sonya in the drawing room, he blushed. He didn't know how to behave around her. The night before, in the first joyful moment of reunion, they had kissed. But today that felt impossible. He sensed that everyone — his mother, his sisters, all of them — was watching him, waiting to see how he would act with her. He kissed her hand and addressed her formally. But their eyes met and spoke intimately, exchanging tender, silent kisses. Her gaze asked forgiveness for having dared, through Natasha, to remind him of his promise — and thanked him for his love. His gaze thanked her for offering him his freedom and told her that one way or another, he would never stop loving her, because that would be impossible.
"How strange," said Vera, choosing a moment when everyone was silent, "that Sonya and Nicholas now address each other formally and act like strangers."

Vera's observation was accurate, as her remarks always were. But like most of her comments, it made everyone uncomfortable — not just Sonya, Nicholas, and Natasha, but even the old countess, who dreaded this love affair that might prevent Nicholas from making a brilliant match. She blushed like a young girl.

Denisov, to Rostov's surprise, appeared in the drawing room with pomaded hair, wearing cologne and a new uniform, looking as sharp as he made himself before going into battle. He was more charming with the ladies and gentlemen than Rostov had ever seen him.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Prince Andrew needed to see the district marshal of the nobility in connection with his son's Ryazan estate. This marshal was Count Ilya Rostov, and in the middle of May, Prince Andrew went to visit him.
It was now hot spring weather. The forest was fully green. It was dusty and so warm that passing any water made you long to bathe.

Prince Andrew, preoccupied and gloomy about the business he needed to discuss with the marshal, was driving up the avenue to the Rostovs' house at Otradnoe. He heard merry girlish cries from behind some trees to the right and saw a group of girls running across the path of his carriage. Ahead of the others, nearest to him, ran a dark-haired, remarkably slim, pretty girl in a yellow cotton dress with a white kerchief on her head, from under which loose locks of hair had escaped. The girl was shouting something but, seeing a stranger, ran back laughing without looking at him.

Suddenly, and he didn't know why, he felt a pang. The day was so beautiful, the sun so bright, everything around so cheerful — and that slim, pretty girl didn't know or care that he existed. She was content and happy in her own separate — probably silly — but bright and joyful life. "What is she so glad about? What is she thinking of? Not about military regulations or the arrangement of the Ryazan serfs' rents. What is she thinking? Why is she so happy?" Prince Andrew asked himself with involuntary curiosity.

In 1809 Count Ilya Rostov was living at Otradnoe just as in previous years — entertaining nearly the whole province with hunts, theatricals, dinners, and music. He was glad to see Prince Andrew, as he was to see any new visitor, and insisted he stay the night.

During the tedious day, in the course of which he was entertained by his elderly hosts and the more important visitors — the old count's house was packed in anticipation of a name-day celebration — Prince Andrew kept glancing at Natasha, who was gay and laughing among the younger guests, and each time he asked himself: "What is she thinking about? Why is she so happy?"

That night, alone in unfamiliar surroundings, he was long unable to sleep. He read for a while, then put out his candle — then relit it. It was hot in the room, with the shutters closed. He was annoyed at the foolish old man (as he called Rostov) who had kept him there by insisting that some necessary documents hadn't arrived from town, and he was annoyed at himself for having stayed.
