He got up and went to the window to open it. The moment he opened the shutters, the moonlight — as if it had been waiting for this — flooded into the room. He opened the casement. The night was cool, bright, and perfectly still. Just below the window stood a row of pollard trees, black on one side, silvery on the other. Beneath them grew some kind of lush, wet, bushy vegetation with silver-touched leaves and stems here and there. Further off, beyond the dark trees, a roof glistened with dew; to the right rose a great leafy tree with brilliantly white trunk and branches, and above it shone the moon, nearly full, in a pale, almost starless spring sky. Prince Andrew leaned his elbows on the window ledge and let his gaze rest on that sky.
His room was on the first floor. Those in the rooms above were awake too. He heard female voices overhead.
"Just once more," said a girlish voice above him that Prince Andrew recognized at once.
"But when are you going to bed?" replied another voice.
"I won't! I can't sleep — what's the use? Come on, one last time."
Two girlish voices sang a musical passage — the ending of some song.
"Oh, how lovely! Now go to sleep — that's it."

"You go to sleep, but I can't," said the first voice, coming nearer to the window. She was evidently leaning right out, because the rustle of her dress and even her breathing could be heard. Everything was stone-still — like the moon and its light and the shadows. Prince Andrew, too, dared not stir, afraid of revealing his presence.

"Sonya! Sonya!" he heard the first voice again. "Oh, how can you sleep! Just look how gorgeous it is! Oh, how gorgeous! Wake up, Sonya!" she said, almost in tears. "There has never, never been such a beautiful night!"
Sonya murmured something reluctant in reply.

"Come look at the moon! Oh, how lovely! Come here, darling, sweetheart, come here! See? I feel like crouching down on my heels and hugging my knees like this, pulling tight — as tight as I can — and flying away! Like this..."
"Careful — you'll fall out."
He heard the sound of a scuffle and Sonya's disapproving voice: "It's past one o'clock."
"Oh, you just ruin everything. Fine — go, go!"
Again all was silent, but Prince Andrew knew she was still sitting there. From time to time he heard a soft rustle, and once a sigh.
"Oh God! Oh God! What does it mean?" she suddenly exclaimed. "Well, off to bed then, if I must!" And she slammed the window shut.

"I might as well not exist for her!" thought Prince Andrew as he listened, for some reason expecting — and fearing — that she might say something about him. "There she is again! As if it were on purpose," he thought.

In his soul there suddenly arose such an unexpected turmoil of youthful thoughts and hopes — so contrary to the whole direction of his life — that, unable to make sense of his own state, he lay down and fell asleep at once.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: During that year after his son's departure, old Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky's health and temper grew much worse. He became still more irritable, and it was Princess Mary who usually bore the brunt of his frequent fits of unprovoked anger. He seemed to search deliberately for her most sensitive spots in order to torment her mentally as cruelly as possible. Princess Mary had two passions and therefore two sources of joy — her nephew, little Nicholas, and religion — and these were the old prince's favorite targets for mockery and attack. Whatever the topic of conversation, he would steer it around to the superstitions of old maids or the pampering and spoiling of children. "You want to turn him" — little Nicholas — "into an old maid like yourself! A pity! Prince Andrew wants a son, not an old maid," he would say. Or, turning to Mademoiselle Bourienne, he would ask her in Princess Mary's presence how she liked their village priests and icons, and would joke about them.

He continually hurt Princess Mary and tormented her, but it cost her no effort to forgive him. Could he really be to blame? Could her father, whom she knew loved her in spite of everything, truly be unjust? And what is justice? The princess never dwelt on that proud word "justice." All the complex laws of humanity were reduced for her into one clear and simple law — the law of love and self-sacrifice taught by Him who lovingly suffered for mankind though He Himself was God. What did she have to do with the justice or injustice of other people? She had to endure and love, and that is what she did.

During the winter Prince Andrew had come to Bald Hills and had been gay, gentle, and more affectionate than Princess Mary had known him in a long time. She felt that something had happened to him, but he told her nothing about his love. Before he left he had a long conversation with his father about something, and Princess Mary noticed that before his departure they were dissatisfied with one another.

Soon after Prince Andrew's departure, Princess Mary wrote to her friend Julie Karagina in Petersburg — the one she had dreamed, as all girls do, of marrying to her brother — who was at that time in mourning for her own brother, killed in Turkey.
Sorrow, it seems, is our common lot, my dear, tender friend Julie.

Your loss is so terrible that I can only explain it as a special act of God's providence — He who, loving you, wishes to try you and your excellent mother. Oh, my friend! Religion, and religion alone, can — I will not say comfort us — but save us from despair. Religion alone can explain what without its help we cannot comprehend: why kind and noble people who could find happiness in life — who harm no one and are necessary to the happiness of others — are called away to God, while cruel, useless, harmful people, or those who are a burden to themselves and to everyone around them, are left alive. The first death I ever witnessed, one I shall never forget — that of my dear sister-in-law — left that impression on me. Just as you ask fate why your wonderful brother had to die, so I asked why that angel Lise, who never wronged anyone and in whose soul there was never an unkind thought, had to die. And what do you think, dear friend? Five years have passed since then, and I, with my small understanding, am beginning to see clearly why she had to die, and in what way that death was an expression of the infinite goodness of the Creator, whose every action, though generally incomprehensible to us, is nothing but a manifestation of His infinite love for His creatures. Perhaps, I often think, she was too angelically innocent to have the strength to fulfill all a mother's duties. As a young wife she was irreproachable; perhaps she could not have been so as a mother. As it is, she has not only left us — and particularly Prince Andrew — with the purest memories and regrets, but she will likely receive there a place I dare not hope for myself. But to speak not of her alone — that early and terrible death has had the most beneficial influence on me and on my brother despite all our grief. Then, at the moment of our loss, these thoughts would never have occurred to me; I would have dismissed them with horror. But now they are very clear and certain. I write all this to you, dear friend, only to convince you of the Gospel truth which has become the guiding principle of my life: not a single hair of our heads will fall without His will. And His will is governed only by infinite love for us, and so whatever happens to us is for our good.

You ask whether we shall spend next winter in Moscow. Despite my wish to see you, I don't think so and don't want to. You will be surprised to hear that the reason is Bonaparte! Here is why: my father's health is growing noticeably worse; he cannot tolerate any contradiction and is becoming irritable. This irritability is, as you know, directed mainly at political matters. He cannot endure the idea that Bonaparte is negotiating on equal terms with all the sovereigns of Europe, and especially with ours, the grandson of the Great Catherine! As you know, I am quite indifferent to politics, but from my father's conversations and his talks with Michael Ivanovich I know everything that goes on in the world, and especially about the honors being heaped on Bonaparte — who, it seems, is accepted everywhere in the world as a great man and even Emperor of France, everywhere except at Bald Hills. And my father cannot bear it. It seems to me that it is mainly because of his political views that my father is reluctant to speak of going to Moscow; for he foresees the confrontations that would result from his habit of expressing his opinions without regard for anyone. Any benefit he might get from medical treatment he would lose in the arguments about Bonaparte that would be unavoidable. In any case the matter will be decided very soon.

Our family life goes on as before, except for my brother Andrew's absence. He, as I wrote to you before, has changed very much of late. After his grief, it was only this year that he truly recovered his spirits. He has become again as I knew him when we were children: kind, affectionate, with that heart of gold for which I know no equal. He has realized, it seems to me, that life is not over for him. But along with this inner change he has grown physically much weaker. He has become thinner and more nervous. I worry about him and am glad he is taking this trip abroad that his doctors have long recommended. I hope it will restore his health. You write that in Petersburg he is spoken of as one of the most active, cultivated, and capable of the young men. Forgive my family pride, but I never doubted it. The good he has done for everyone here, from his peasants to the gentry, is incalculable. On his arrival in Petersburg he received only his due. I am always amazed at the way rumors fly from Petersburg to Moscow, especially false ones such as the one you mention — that my brother is engaged to the little Rostova. I do not think my brother will ever marry again, and certainly not her; and this is why: first, I know that though he rarely speaks of the wife he lost, the grief of that loss has gone too deep in his heart for him ever to give her a successor and our little angel a stepmother. Second, as far as I know, that girl is not the kind who could please Prince Andrew. I do not think he would choose her for a wife, and frankly I would not wish it. But I am going on too long and am at the end of my second sheet. Goodbye, my dear friend. May God keep you in His holy and mighty care. My dear friend Mademoiselle Bourienne sends you kisses.
MARY

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: From Smolensk the troops continued to retreat, with the enemy in pursuit. On the tenth of August the regiment Prince Andrew commanded was marching along the highway past the avenue leading to Bald Hills. Heat and drought had continued for more than three weeks. Each day fluffy clouds floated across the sky and occasionally veiled the sun, but toward evening the sky cleared again and the sun set in reddish-brown mist. Heavy night dews alone refreshed the earth. The unharvested grain was scorched and shedding its seeds. The marshes dried up. The cattle lowed from hunger, finding no food on the sun-parched meadows. Only at night and in the forests, while the dew lasted, was there any freshness. But on the road—the highway along which the troops marched—there was no freshness even at night or when the road passed through forest; the dew was imperceptible on the sandy dust churned up more than six inches deep. As soon as day dawned, the march began. The artillery and baggage wagons moved silently through the deep dust that rose to the very wheel hubs, and the infantry sank ankle-deep in that soft, choking, hot dust that never cooled even at night. Some of this dust was kneaded by feet and wheels, while the rest rose and hung like a cloud over the troops, settling in eyes, ears, hair, and nostrils, and worst of all in the lungs of men and animals as they moved along that road. The higher the sun rose, the higher rose that cloud of dust, and through the screen of its hot fine particles one could look with the naked eye at the sun, which showed like a huge crimson ball in the unclouded sky. There was no wind, and the men choked in that motionless air. They marched with handkerchiefs tied over their noses and mouths. When they passed through a village, they all rushed to the wells and fought for the water, drinking it down to the mud.

Prince Andrew was in command of a regiment, and the management of that regiment—the welfare of the men and the necessity of receiving and giving orders—absorbed him entirely. The burning of Smolensk and its abandonment marked an epoch in his life. A new feeling of anger against the enemy made him forget his own sorrow. He devoted himself entirely to the affairs of his regiment and was considerate and kind to his men and officers. In the regiment they called him "our prince," were proud of him, and loved him. But he was kind and gentle only to those of his regiment, to Timokhin and the like—people completely new to him, belonging to a different world, who could not know or understand his past. As soon as he encountered a former acquaintance or anyone from the staff, he bristled up at once and became spiteful, ironic, and contemptuous. Everything that reminded him of his past was repugnant to him, and so in his relations with that former world he confined himself to trying to do his duty and not be unfair.

In truth, everything presented itself in a dark and gloomy light to Prince Andrew, especially after the abandonment of Smolensk on the sixth of August (he believed it could and should have been defended) and after his sick father had been forced to flee to Moscow, leaving his beloved Bald Hills—which he had built and populated—to be plundered. But despite this, thanks to his regiment, Prince Andrew had something to think about that was entirely separate from general questions. Two days earlier he had received news that his father, son, and sister had left for Moscow; and though there was nothing for him to do at Bald Hills, Prince Andrew, with a characteristic desire to aggravate his own grief, decided he had to ride there.

He ordered his horse saddled and, leaving his regiment on the march, rode to his father's estate where he had been born and spent his childhood. Riding past the pond where there had always been dozens of women chattering as they rinsed their laundry or beat it with wooden paddles, Prince Andrew noticed there wasn't a soul about, and the little washing dock, torn from its place and half submerged, was floating on its side in the middle of the pond. He rode to the gatekeeper's lodge. No one was at the stone entrance gates of the drive and the door was open. Grass had already begun to grow on the garden paths, and horses and calves were wandering through the English park. Prince Andrew rode up to the greenhouse; some of the glass panes were broken, and some of the trees in tubs were overturned, others dried up. He called for Taras the gardener, but no one replied. Having gone around the corner of the greenhouse to the ornamental garden, he saw that the carved garden fence was broken and branches of the plum trees had been torn off with the fruit. An old peasant whom Prince Andrew had often seen at the gate in his childhood was sitting on a green garden seat, weaving a bast shoe.

He was deaf and didn't hear Prince Andrew ride up. He was sitting on the bench the old prince used to like to sit on, and beside him strips of bast were hanging on the broken and withered branch of a magnolia.

Prince Andrew rode up to the house. Several lime trees in the old garden had been cut down, and a piebald mare and her foal were wandering among the rosebushes in front of the house. The shutters were all closed except at one open window. A little servant boy, seeing Prince Andrew, ran into the house. Alpatych, having sent his family away, was alone at Bald Hills, sitting indoors reading the Lives of the Saints. On hearing that Prince Andrew had come, he went out with his spectacles on his nose, buttoning his coat, and hastily stepping up, without a word began weeping and kissing Prince Andrew's knee.

Then, vexed at his own weakness, he turned away and began reporting on the state of affairs. Everything precious and valuable had been moved to Bogucharovo. Seventy quarters of grain had also been carted away. The hay and the spring grain, of which Alpatych said there had been a remarkable crop that year, had been commandeered by the troops and mowed down while still green. The peasants were ruined; some had also gone to Bogucharovo, and only a few remained.
Without waiting to hear him finish, Prince Andrew asked:
"When did my father and sister leave?"—meaning when did they leave for Moscow.

Alpatych, understanding the question to be about their departure for Bogucharovo, replied that they had left on the seventh, and again went into details about the estate management, asking for instructions.
"Should I let the troops have the oats and take a receipt? We still have six hundred quarters left," he asked.

"What can I tell him?" thought Prince Andrew, looking down at the old man's bald head shining in the sun and seeing from his expression that the old man himself understood how out of place these questions were and only asked them to ease his grief.
"Yes, let them have it," replied Prince Andrew.

"If you noticed some disorder in the garden," said Alpatych, "it was impossible to prevent. Three regiments came through and spent the night—dragoons, mostly. I took down the name and rank of their commanding officer so I could file a complaint."
"Well, what are you going to do? Stay here if the enemy occupies the place?" asked Prince Andrew.
Alpatych turned his face to Prince Andrew, looked at him, and suddenly with a solemn gesture raised his arm.
"He is my refuge! His will be done!" he exclaimed.
A group of bareheaded peasants was approaching across the meadow toward the prince.
"Well, goodbye!" said Prince Andrew, bending down to Alpatych. "You must leave too—take away what you can, and tell the serfs to go to the Ryazan estate or to the one near Moscow."
Alpatych clung to Prince Andrew's leg and burst into sobs. Gently freeing himself, the prince spurred his horse and galloped down the avenue.

The old man was still sitting in the ornamental garden, like a fly sitting motionless on the face of a loved one who is dead, tapping the shoe last on which he was weaving the bast shoe, and two little girls, running out from the greenhouse carrying plums they had picked in their skirts, came upon Prince Andrew. Seeing the young master, the older one seized her younger companion by the hand with a frightened look and hid with her behind a birch tree, not stopping to pick up some green plums they had dropped.

Prince Andrew turned away with startled haste, unwilling to let them see they had been noticed. He felt sorry for the pretty frightened little girl, was afraid of looking at her, and yet felt an irresistible desire to do so. A new sensation of comfort and relief came over him when, seeing these girls, he realized that other human interests existed entirely apart from his own and just as legitimate as those that consumed him. These girls clearly wanted nothing more passionately than to carry away and eat those green plums without getting caught—and Prince Andrew shared their wish for the success of their enterprise. He couldn't resist looking at them once more. Believing the danger had passed, they sprang from their hiding place and, chirping something in their shrill little voices and holding up their skirts, scampered merrily and quickly on their bare, sunburned feet across the meadow grass.

Prince Andrew felt somewhat refreshed from having ridden off the dusty highway along which the troops were moving. But not far from Bald Hills he came back to the road and overtook his regiment at its halt by the dam of a small pond. It was past one o'clock. The sun, a red ball through the dust, burned and scorched his back unbearably through his black coat. The dust always hung motionless above the buzz of talk from the resting troops. There was no wind. As he crossed the dam, Prince Andrew caught the smell of ooze and freshness from the pond. He longed to get into that water, however dirty it might be, and he glanced at the pond from which came sounds of shrieks and laughter. The small, muddy, green pond had risen visibly more than a foot above the dam, because it was full of naked white bodies of soldiers with sunburned hands, necks, and faces, splashing about in it. All this naked white human flesh, laughing and shrieking, floundered about in that dirty pool like fish stuffed into a watering can, and the suggestion of merriment in that floundering mass made it all the more pitiful.

One fair-haired young soldier of the third company, whom Prince Andrew knew and who had a strap around the calf of one leg, crossed himself, stepped back to get a running start, and plunged into the water; another, a dark noncommissioned officer who was always shaggy, stood waist-deep in the water joyfully flexing his muscular figure and snorted with satisfaction as he poured water over his head with hands blackened to the wrists. There were sounds of men slapping one another, yelling, and spluttering.

Everywhere on the bank, on the dam, and in the pond, there was healthy, white, muscular flesh. The officer Timokhin, with his little red nose, standing on the dam drying himself with a towel, felt embarrassed at seeing the prince but made up his mind to address him anyway.
"It's really nice, your excellency! Wouldn't you like to?" he said.
"It's dirty," replied Prince Andrew, making a face.
"We'll clear it out for you in a minute," said Timokhin, and, still undressed, ran off to clear the men out of the pond.
"The prince wants to bathe."
"What prince? Ours?" said many voices, and the men were in such a hurry to clear out that the prince could barely stop them. He decided he would rather wash himself with water in the barn.

"Flesh, bodies, cannon fodder!" he thought, looking at his own naked body and shuddering—not from cold but from a feeling of disgust and horror he didn't fully understand, aroused by the sight of that immense number of bodies splashing in the dirty pond.
On the seventh of August, Prince Bagration wrote as follows from his quarters at Mikhailovka on the Smolensk road:
Dear Count Alexei Andreevich—(He was writing to Arakcheev but knew the letter would be read by the Emperor, so he weighed every word as carefully as he could.)

I expect the Minister (Barclay de Tolly) has already reported the abandonment of Smolensk to the enemy. It is pitiable and sad, and the whole army is in despair that this most important place has been needlessly abandoned. I, for my part, begged him personally and most urgently, and finally wrote to him, but nothing would persuade him. I swear to you on my honor that Napoleon was in a tighter spot than ever before and might have lost half his army but could not have taken Smolensk. Our troops fought, and are fighting, as never before. With fifteen thousand men I held the enemy at bay for thirty-five hours and beat him; but he would not hold out even for fourteen hours. It is a disgrace, a stain on our army, and as for him, it seems to me he should not go on living. If he reports that our losses were heavy, it is not true; perhaps about four thousand, not more, and not even that; but even were they ten thousand, that's war! But the enemy has lost far more...

What would it have cost him to hold out for another two days? They would have had to retreat on their own, for they had no water for men or horses. He gave me his word he would not retreat, but suddenly sent orders that he was pulling out that night. We cannot fight this way, or we'll soon bring the enemy right to Moscow...

There is a rumor that you are thinking of peace. God forbid that you should make peace after all our sacrifices and such insane retreats! You would turn all Russia against you, and every one of us would be ashamed to wear the uniform. If it has come to this—we must fight as long as Russia stands and as long as there are men able to fight...

One man ought to be in command, not two. Your Minister may perhaps be a good minister, but as a general he is not merely bad but execrable, yet the fate of our whole country has been entrusted to him... I am truly beside myself with frustration; forgive my writing bluntly. It is clear that whoever advocates making peace, and that the Minister should command the army, does not love our sovereign and desires the ruin of us all. So I write to you frankly: call up the militia. For the Minister is leading these visitors of ours straight to Moscow in the most masterly way. The whole army regards the Imperial aide-de-camp Wolzogen with the greatest suspicion. He is said to be more Napoleon's man than ours, and he is forever advising the Minister. I am not merely civil to him but obey him like a corporal, though I am his senior. This is painful, but loving my benefactor and sovereign, I submit. Only I am sorry for the Emperor, that he entrusts our fine army to such a man... Consider that on our retreat we have lost through exhaustion and left in hospitals more than fifteen thousand men, and had we attacked this would not have happened. Tell me, for God's sake, what will Russia—our mother Russia—say to our being so frightened? And why are we abandoning our good and brave Fatherland to such rabble, planting feelings of hatred and shame in all our people? What are we scared of and whom are we afraid of? It is not my fault that the Minister is indecisive, cowardly, dense, slow, and has every bad quality. The whole army weeps over it and curses him...

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: After her father's funeral, Princess Mary shut herself up in her room and refused to see anyone. A maid came to the door to say that Alpatych was asking for orders about their departure. (This was before his talk with Dron.) Princess Mary raised herself from the sofa where she had been lying and replied through the closed door that she didn't intend to go anywhere and asked to be left in peace.

The windows of the room where she lay faced west. She lay on the sofa with her face to the wall, fingering the buttons of the leather cushion and seeing nothing but that cushion, and her confused thoughts centered on one subject—the finality of death and her own spiritual baseness, which she had not suspected but which had revealed itself during her father's illness. She wanted to pray but didn't dare—couldn't, in her present state of mind, address herself to God. She lay there for a long time.

The sun had moved to the other side of the house, and its slanting rays shone through the open window, lighting up the room and part of the leather cushion Princess Mary was looking at. The flow of her thoughts suddenly stopped. Unconsciously she sat up, smoothed her hair, got up, and went to the window, involuntarily breathing in the freshness of the clear but windy evening.
"Yes, you can enjoy the evening now! He's gone and no one will stand in your way," she said to herself, and sinking into a chair, she let her head fall on the windowsill.

Someone spoke her name in a soft and tender voice from the garden and kissed her head. She looked up. It was Mademoiselle Bourienne in a black dress and mourning cap. She softly approached Princess Mary, sighed, kissed her, and immediately began to cry. The princess looked at her. All their former friction and her own jealousy came back to her mind. But she also remembered how he had changed lately toward Mademoiselle Bourienne and could no longer bear the sight of her—showing how unjust the reproaches Princess Mary had mentally leveled at her had been. "Besides, is it for me—I who wished for his death—to condemn anyone?" she thought.

Princess Mary vividly pictured to herself the position of Mademoiselle Bourienne, whom she had recently kept at a distance but who was still dependent on her and living in her house. She felt sorry for her and held out her hand with a look of gentle inquiry. Mademoiselle Bourienne immediately began crying again and kissed that hand, speaking of the princess's sorrow and claiming a share in it. She said her only consolation was that the princess allowed her to share her grief, that all the old misunderstandings should vanish before this great sorrow; that she felt herself blameless toward everyone, and that he, from above, saw her devotion and gratitude. The princess listened, not following the words but occasionally looking up at her and listening to the sound of her voice.

"Your position is doubly terrible, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne after a pause. "I understand that you could not, and cannot, think of yourself, but with my love for you I must do so... Has Alpatych been to you? Has he spoken to you of leaving?" she asked.
Princess Mary did not answer. She didn't understand who was supposed to go or where. "Is it possible to plan or think about anything now? Does anything matter?" she thought, and made no reply.

"You know, dear Marie," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that we are in danger—we are surrounded by the French. It would be dangerous to move now. If we try to go, we will almost certainly be taken prisoner, and God knows..."
Princess Mary looked at her companion without understanding what she was saying.

"Oh, if anyone knew how little anything matters to me now," she said. "Of course I would never want to leave him... Alpatych did say something about going... Speak to him; I can do nothing, nothing, and don't want to..."

"I've spoken to him. He hopes we can still get away tomorrow, but I think it would be better to stay here now," said Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Because, you must agree, dear Marie, to fall into the hands of soldiers or riotous peasants would be terrible."

Mademoiselle Bourienne took from her bag a proclamation (not printed on standard Russian paper) by General Rameau, telling people not to leave their homes and promising that the French authorities would provide proper protection. She handed it to the princess.
"I think it would be best to appeal to that general," she continued. "I'm sure that you would be shown all due respect."
Princess Mary read the paper, and her face began to quiver with stifled sobs.
"Who gave you this?" she asked.
"They probably recognized that I am French, by my name," replied Mademoiselle Bourienne, blushing.
Princess Mary, paper in hand, rose from the window and with a pale face walked out of the room and into what had been Prince Andrew's study.

"Dunyasha! Send Alpatych, or Dronushka, or somebody to me!" she said, "and tell Mademoiselle Bourienne not to come to me," she added, hearing Mademoiselle Bourienne's voice. "We must go at once, at once!" she said, appalled at the thought of being left to the mercy of the French.

"If Prince Andrew found out I was in the power of the French! That I, the daughter of Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky, asked General Rameau for protection and accepted his favor!" This idea horrified her, made her shudder, blush, and feel a surge of anger and pride unlike anything she had ever experienced. All that was distressing, and especially all that was humiliating, in her position rose vividly to her mind. "They, the French, would settle in this house; Monsieur le General Rameau would occupy Prince Andrew's study and amuse himself looking through his letters and papers. Mademoiselle Bourienne would play hostess for him at Bogucharovo. I would be given a small room as a favor; the soldiers would desecrate my father's freshly dug grave to steal his medals and decorations; they would tell me about their victories over the Russians and pretend to sympathize with my grief..." thought Princess Mary, not thinking her own thoughts but feeling compelled to think like her father and brother. For herself she didn't care where she stayed or what happened to her, but she felt herself the representative of her dead father and Prince Andrew. Involuntarily she thought their thoughts and felt their feelings. What they would have said and done, she felt bound to say and do. She went into Prince Andrew's study, trying to enter fully into his way of thinking, and considered her situation.
The demands of life, which had seemed annihilated by her father's death, suddenly rose before her with a new, previously unknown force and took hold of her.

Agitated and flushed, she paced the room, sending now for Michael Ivanovich and now for Tikhon or Dron. Dunyasha, the nurse, and the other maids couldn't say how accurate Mademoiselle Bourienne's claims were. Alpatych was not at home—he had gone to the police. Nor could the architect Michael Ivanovich, who came in with sleepy eyes when sent for, tell Princess Mary anything. With exactly the same smile of agreement with which he had been accustomed to respond to the old prince for fifteen years without expressing opinions of his own, he now answered Princess Mary so that nothing definite could be gathered from his replies. The old valet Tikhon, with his sunken, gaunt face bearing the stamp of inconsolable grief, replied "Yes, Princess" to all her questions and could barely hold back his sobs as he looked at her.
At length Dron, the village Elder, entered the room and with a deep bow to Princess Mary came to a halt by the doorpost.
Princess Mary walked up and down the room and stopped in front of him.

"Dronushka," she said, regarding as a trusted friend this man who always used to bring a special kind of gingerbread from his trips to the Vyazma fair every year and smilingly offer it to her, "Dronushka, now after our misfortune..." she began, but could not go on.
"We are all in God's hands," he said with a sigh.
They were silent for a while.
"Dronushka, Alpatych has gone off somewhere and I have no one to turn to. Is it true, as they tell me, that I can't even leave?"
"Why shouldn't you leave, your excellency? You can go," said Dron.
"I was told it would be dangerous because of the enemy. Dear friend, I can't manage anything. I don't understand anything. I have nobody! I want to go away tonight or early tomorrow morning."
Dron paused. He glanced sideways at Princess Mary and said: "There are no horses; I told Yakov Alpatych so."
"Why are there none?" asked the princess.

"It's all God's punishment," said Dron. "Whatever horses we had were taken for the army or died—it's been that kind of year! We can barely feed ourselves, let alone keep horses. Some go three days without eating. We've got nothing—we've been ruined."
Princess Mary listened carefully to what he told her.
"The peasants are ruined? They have no bread?" she asked.
"They're starving," said Dron. "It's not a matter of carting."
"But why didn't you tell me, Dronushka? Can't something be done to help them? I'll do everything I can..."

To Princess Mary it seemed strange that now, at a moment when such sorrow filled her soul, there could be rich and poor, and that the rich could fail to help the poor. She vaguely knew there was such a thing as "landlord's grain" that was sometimes given to the peasants. She also knew that neither her father nor her brother would refuse to help peasants in need; she only feared making some mistake in distributing the grain she wanted to give. She was glad that such practical concerns presented themselves, allowing her without guilt to forget her own grief. She began asking Dron about the peasants' needs and what belonged to the landlord at Bogucharovo.
"But we have grain belonging to my brother?" she said.
"The landlord's grain is all safe," replied Dron proudly. "Our prince gave no order to sell it."
"Give it to the peasants—let them have everything they need; I give you permission in my brother's name," she said.
Dron said nothing but sighed deeply.
"Give them that grain if there's enough. Distribute it all. I give this order in my brother's name; and tell them that what is ours is theirs. We don't grudge them anything. Tell them that."
Dron looked hard at the princess while she was speaking.
"Let me go, dear lady, for God's sake! Order the keys to be taken from me," he said. "I've served twenty-three years and done no wrong. Let me go, for God's sake!"

Princess Mary didn't understand what he wanted or why he was asking to be discharged. She replied that she had never doubted his devotion and that she was ready to do anything for him and for the peasants.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: The forces of a dozen European nations burst into Russia. The Russian army and people avoided a collision until Smolensk, and again from Smolensk to Borodino. The French army pushed on toward Moscow, its goal, its momentum ever increasing as it neared its aim — just as the speed of a falling body increases as it approaches the earth. Behind it lay seven hundred miles of hunger-stricken, hostile country; ahead lay just a few dozen miles to its goal. Every soldier in Napoleon's army felt this, and the invasion moved forward under its own momentum.

The more the Russian army retreated, the more fiercely a spirit of hatred for the enemy flared up, and as it fell back, the army grew and consolidated. At Borodino, a collision occurred. Neither army was shattered, but the Russian army retreated immediately after the clash as inevitably as a ball bounces back after striking another with greater momentum, and with equal inevitability the ball of invasion — which had advanced with such force — rolled on for some distance, even though the collision had stripped it of all its power.

The Russians retreated eighty miles — beyond Moscow — and the French reached Moscow, where they came to a standstill. For five weeks there was not a single battle. The French didn't move. Like a mortally wounded animal licking its wounds, they remained inert in Moscow for five weeks. Then suddenly, for no fresh reason, they fled back — dashing for the Kaluga road, and after a victory (at Malo-Yaroslavets, where the field of battle remained theirs) without fighting a single serious engagement, they retreated even faster toward Smolensk, beyond Smolensk, beyond the Berezina, beyond Vilna, and farther still.

On the evening of August 26, Kutuzov and the entire Russian army were convinced that the Battle of Borodino was a victory. Kutuzov reported this to the Emperor. He gave orders to prepare for a fresh battle to finish off the enemy, and did so not to deceive anyone but because he knew the enemy had been beaten — as everyone who had fought in the battle knew.
But all that evening and the next day, reports came in one after another of unheard-of losses — the loss of half the army — and a fresh battle proved physically impossible.

It was impossible to fight before information was gathered, the wounded collected, ammunition supplies replenished, the dead counted, new officers appointed to replace those killed, and the men had eaten and slept. And meanwhile, the very next morning, the French army advanced on its own, carried forward by its momentum — now seemingly increased in inverse proportion to the square of the distance from its goal. Kutuzov wanted to attack the next day, and the whole army wanted the same. But wanting to attack is not enough — there must also be the ability to do so, and that ability did not exist. It was impossible not to retreat one day's march, and then in the same way it was impossible not to retreat another day's march, and a third, and at last, on September 1, when the army drew near Moscow — despite the powerful feelings that had risen in every rank — circumstances forced it to retreat beyond Moscow. And the troops made one final day's march and abandoned Moscow to the enemy.

For people accustomed to thinking that campaign plans and battles are made by generals — as any of us, sitting over a map in a study, can imagine how we'd have arranged things in this or that battle — certain questions arise: Why didn't Kutuzov do this or that during the retreat? Why didn't he take up a position before reaching Fili? Why didn't he retreat at once by the Kaluga road, abandoning Moscow? People who think this way forget, or don't know, the inevitable constraints that always limit any commander in chief. The activity of a commander in chief bears no resemblance to what we imagine when sitting comfortably at our desks studying a campaign on a map, with known numbers of troops on each side in a known location, starting from a given moment. A commander in chief never deals with the beginning of any event — the starting point from which we always view it. He is always in the midst of a series of shifting events, and at no moment can he grasp the full significance of what is happening. From moment to moment the event takes shape imperceptibly, and at every instant the commander in chief finds himself in the middle of a complex web of intrigues, worries, contingencies, authorities, projects, counsels, threats, and deceptions, constantly forced to respond to countless questions that conflict with one another.

Military scholars solemnly tell us that Kutuzov should have moved his army to the Kaluga road long before reaching Fili, and that somebody actually proposed this to him. But a commander in chief, especially in a difficult moment, always faces not one proposal but dozens simultaneously. And all these proposals, based on strategy and tactics, contradict each other.

A commander in chief's job might seem to be simply choosing one of these proposals. But he cannot even do that. Events and time do not wait. For instance, on the twenty-eighth, someone suggests crossing to the Kaluga road, but just then an adjutant gallops up from Miloradovich asking whether to engage the French or retreat. An order must be given instantly. And the order to retreat carries them past the turn to the Kaluga road. After the adjutant comes the supply officer asking where to send the provisions, then the head of hospitals asking where to send the wounded, then a courier from Petersburg with a letter from the sovereign refusing to contemplate abandoning Moscow. The commander in chief's rival — the man undermining him (and there are always several such men, not just one) — presents a new plan diametrically opposed to the Kaluga road idea. The commander in chief needs sleep and refreshment. A respected general overlooked in the distribution of awards comes to complain. Local residents beg for protection. An officer sent to inspect the area reports one thing; a scout, a prisoner, and a general from reconnaissance all describe the enemy's position differently. People accustomed to misunderstanding or forgetting these inevitable constraints describe, for instance, the army's position at Fili and assume the commander in chief could freely decide on September 1 whether to abandon or defend Moscow — whereas with the Russian army less than four miles away, no such question existed. When had it been decided? At Drissa, at Smolensk, and most clearly of all on August 24 at Shevardino and the twenty-sixth at Borodino, and every day, hour, and minute of the retreat from Borodino to Fili.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: On Saturday, August 31, everything in the Rostov house seemed topsy-turvy. All the doors were open, all the furniture was being carried out or rearranged, and the mirrors and pictures had been taken down. Trunks stood in the rooms, and hay, wrapping paper, and rope were scattered about. The peasants and house servants carrying things out trod heavily on the parquet floors. The yard was crowded with peasant carts — some loaded high and already roped up, others still empty.

The voices and footsteps of the many servants and the peasants who'd come with the carts echoed through the yard and house as they shouted to one another. The count had been out since morning. The countess, with a headache from all the noise and chaos, lay in the new sitting room with a vinegar compress on her forehead. Petya wasn't home — he'd gone to see a friend about getting a transfer from the militia to the active army. Sonya was in the ballroom overseeing the packing of glassware and china. Natasha sat on the floor of her dismantled room amid scattered dresses, ribbons, and scarves, staring at the floor and holding in her hands the old ball gown — already out of fashion — that she'd worn to her first Petersburg ball.

Natasha was ashamed of doing nothing when everyone else was so busy. Several times that morning she'd tried to help, but her heart wasn't in it, and she simply didn't know how to do anything without giving it her whole heart and soul. For a while she'd stood beside Sonya while the china was being packed and tried to assist, but soon gave up and went to her room to pack her own things. At first she enjoyed giving away dresses and ribbons to the maids, but when that was done and what remained still had to be packed, she found it tedious.

"Dunyasha, you pack it! You will, won't you, dear?" And when Dunyasha cheerfully promised to do it all, Natasha sat down on the floor, took her old ball gown, and drifted into a daydream entirely unrelated to what should have occupied her thoughts. She was roused by the chatter of the maids in the next room and their hurried footsteps toward the back porch. Natasha got up and looked out the window. An enormously long row of carts full of wounded men had stopped in the street.
The housekeeper, the old nurse, the cooks, coachmen, maids, footmen, postilions, and kitchen boys all stood at the gate, staring at the wounded.
Natasha, throwing a clean handkerchief over her hair and holding an end in each hand, went out into the street.

The former housekeeper, old Mavra Kuzminichna, had stepped out from the crowd at the gate and approached a cart with a hood made of bark matting. She was talking to a pale young officer who lay inside. Natasha came a few steps closer and stopped shyly, still holding her handkerchief, listening to what the housekeeper was saying.
"So you have nobody in Moscow?" she was saying. "You'd be more comfortable in a house somewhere — in ours, for instance. The family is leaving."
"I don't know if it would be allowed," the officer replied weakly. "There's our commanding officer — ask him," and he pointed to a stout major walking back along the street past the line of carts.
Natasha glanced with frightened eyes at the wounded officer's face and immediately went to meet the major.
"May the wounded men stay in our house?" she asked.
The major raised his hand to his cap with a smile.
"Which one would you like, miss?" he said, squinting and smiling.

Natasha quietly repeated her question, and her face and whole manner were so serious — though she was still holding the ends of her handkerchief — that the major stopped smiling and, after a moment's reflection, as if weighing whether it could be arranged, answered in the affirmative.
"Oh yes, why not? They may," he said.
With a slight nod, Natasha hurried back to Mavra Kuzminichna, who was still talking sympathetically to the officer.
"They may! He says they may!" she whispered.

The cart carrying the officer was turned into the Rostovs' yard, and at the invitation of the townspeople, dozens of carts with wounded men began pulling into the yards and drawing up at the entrances of houses along Povarskaya Street. Natasha was clearly pleased to be dealing with new people outside her ordinary routine. She and Mavra Kuzminichna tried to get as many wounded as possible into their yard.
"Your papa should be told, though," said Mavra Kuzminichna.
"Never mind, never mind — what does it matter? For one day we can move into the drawing room. They can have our whole half of the house."
"Really now, young lady, the ideas you get! Even if we put them in the wing — the men's room or the nurse's room — we still need permission."
"Well, I'll ask."
Natasha ran into the house and went on tiptoe through the half-open door into the sitting room, where there was a smell of vinegar and Hoffmann's drops.
"Are you asleep, Mama?"
"What sleep?" said the countess, waking up just as she was drifting off.

"Mama, darling!" said Natasha, kneeling by her mother and bringing her face close. "I'm sorry — forgive me — I'll never do it again. I woke you up! Mavra Kuzminichna sent me — they've brought wounded men here, officers. Will you let them stay? They have nowhere to go. I knew you'd say yes!" she said all in one breath.
"What officers? Who's been brought? I don't understand anything," said the countess.
Natasha laughed, and the countess smiled slightly too.
"I knew you'd give permission — so I'll tell them," and, kissing her mother, Natasha jumped up and went to the door.
In the hall she met her father, who had returned with bad news.
"We've stayed too long!" the count said with involuntary irritation. "The Club is closed and the police are leaving."
"Papa, is it all right? I've invited some of the wounded into our house," said Natasha.
"Of course, of course," he answered absently. "That's not the point. Please stop fussing with trifles and help with the packing. Tomorrow we must go — go, go!"
And the count gave similar orders to the major-domo and servants.

At dinner, Petya came home and told them his news. He said people had been collecting weapons at the Kremlin, and though Rostopchin's broadsheet had promised two or three days' warning, the order had already been given for everyone to go armed to the Three Hills tomorrow — there was going to be a big battle there.

The countess looked with timid horror at her son's eager, excited face. She realized that if she said a word about his not going to the battle (she knew how much he relished the thought), he would say something about men, honor, and the fatherland — something senseless, masculine, and unanswerable — and her plans would be ruined. So, hoping to arrange to leave before then and take Petya along as their protector and defender, she said nothing. After dinner, she took the count aside and, in tears, begged him to take her away — that very night if possible. With a woman's instinctive, loving cunning, she who until then had shown no alarm now said she would die of fright if they didn't leave that very night. Without pretending, she was now afraid of everything.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: The Russian troops passed through Moscow from two in the morning until two in the afternoon, carrying the wounded and the last departing residents with them.
The worst congestion occurred at the Stone, Moskva, and Yauza bridges.

While the troops, splitting into two streams around the Kremlin, crowded the Moskva and Stone bridges, a great many soldiers — taking advantage of the delay and gridlock — turned back from the bridges and slipped stealthily and silently past the Church of St. Basil, under the Borovitsky gate, and back up the hill to Red Square, where some instinct told them they could easily help themselves to things that weren't theirs. Crowds like those at a clearance sale filled every passage and alley of the Bazaar. But there were no dealers calling out with ingratiating affability, no hawkers, no usual motley crowd of female shoppers — only soldiers in uniforms and overcoats, though without muskets, entering the Bazaar empty-handed and silently making their way out through the passages with bundles. The shopkeepers and their assistants (of whom very few remained) moved about among the soldiers in bewilderment. They unlocked their shops and locked them again, and carried goods away themselves with the help of their assistants. On the square in front of the Bazaar, drummers beat the muster call. But the drumroll, instead of drawing looting soldiers toward it as it once would have, drove them farther away. Among the soldiers in the shops and passages, men in gray coats with shaved heads could be seen. Two officers — one with a scarf over his uniform mounted on a lean gray horse, the other in an overcoat and on foot — stood at the corner of Ilyinka Street, talking. A third officer galloped up.
"The general orders them all driven out immediately, without fail. This is outrageous! Half the men have scattered."
"Where are you going? Where?" he shouted at three infantrymen without muskets who, holding up the skirts of their overcoats, were slipping past into the Bazaar passage. "Stop, you rascals!"
"But how are you going to stop them?" another officer replied. "There's no rounding them up. The army needs to push on before the rest scatter — that's all!"
"How can we push on? They're stuck on the bridge, jammed solid. Shouldn't we throw a cordon around to keep the rest from running off?"
"Go in there and drive them out!" the senior officer shouted.

The officer in the scarf dismounted, called for a drummer, and went into the arcade. Some soldiers started running away in a group. A shopkeeper with red pimples on his cheeks near his nose, wearing a calm, patient, calculating expression on his plump face, hurried up to the officer, swinging his arms ostentatiously.

"Your honor!" he said. "Please be so kind as to protect us! We won't begrudge trifles — you're welcome to anything, we'd be delighted! Please! I'll fetch a piece of cloth right away for such a distinguished gentleman, or even two, with pleasure. Because we understand the situation — but this here is just plain robbery! If you please, sir, couldn't guards be posted, at least to let us close up shop?"
Several other shopkeepers crowded around the officer.

"Bah, what drivel!" said one of them — a thin, stern-looking man. "When your head's been cut off you don't weep for your hair! Take whatever you want!" And he waved his arm energetically and turned sideways to the officer.
"Easy for you to talk, Ivan Sidorych!" the first tradesman said angrily. "Please step inside, your honor!"

"Talk indeed!" the thin one retorted. "In my three shops I've got a hundred thousand rubles' worth of goods. Can they be saved once the army's gone? Well, people — 'against God's might our hands can't fight.'"
"Come inside, your honor!" the first tradesman repeated, bowing.
The officer stood there, perplexed, indecision on his face.
"It's none of my business!" he exclaimed, and strode quickly down one of the passages.
From one open shop came the sound of blows and cursing, and just as the officer reached it, a man in a gray coat with a shaved head was thrown violently out the door.

The man, doubled over, rushed past the tradesman and the officer. The officer grabbed at the soldiers who were in the shops, but at that moment terrible screams reached them from the huge crowd on the Moskva bridge, and the officer ran out to the square.
"What is it? What's happening?" he asked, but his fellow officer was already galloping past St. Basil's toward the source of the screams.

The officer mounted his horse and rode after him. When he reached the bridge he saw two unlimbered guns, infantry crossing, several overturned carts, and frightened, laughing faces among the troops. Beside the cannon stood a cart harnessed to two horses. Four greyhounds with collars pressed close to the wheels. The cart was piled high, and at the very top — beside a child's chair turned upside down — sat a peasant woman, shrieking piercingly. He was told by his fellow officers that the crowd's screams and the woman's shrieks were caused by General Ermolov, who had ridden up to the crowd and, learning that soldiers were looting the shops while civilians clogged the bridge, had ordered two guns unlimbered and made a show of firing at the bridge. The crowd, crushing one another, overturning carts, screaming and squeezing desperately, had cleared off the bridge, and the troops were now advancing.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: By around nine o'clock in the morning, when the troops were already marching through Moscow, nobody came to the count for instructions anymore. Those who could get away were leaving on their own, and those who stayed behind decided for themselves what they had to do.
The count ordered his carriage so he could drive to Sokolniki, and sat in his study with his hands folded, gloomy, sallow-faced, and silent.

In quiet, untroubled times, every administrator imagines that the entire population under his rule is kept going only by his efforts, and it is this sense of being indispensable that provides the chief reward for his labor. While the sea of history remains calm, the ruler-administrator in his little boat, holding on with a boat hook to the great ship of the people and moving along with it, naturally imagines that his efforts are moving the ship. But as soon as a storm arises and the sea begins to heave, such a delusion becomes impossible. The ship moves on its own with its own enormous force, the boat hook no longer reaches the vessel, and suddenly the administrator—instead of appearing a powerful ruler—becomes an insignificant, useless, feeble man.
Rostopchin felt this, and it was what enraged him.

The superintendent of police, who had been stopped by the crowd, came to see him at the same time as an adjutant who informed the count that the horses were harnessed. They were both pale, and the superintendent, after reporting that he had carried out his instructions, informed the count that a huge crowd had gathered in the courtyard and wanted to see him.

Without saying a word, Rostopchin rose and walked quickly to his elegant, luxurious drawing room, went to the balcony door, took hold of the handle, let it go again, and went to the window from which he could better see the whole crowd. The tall young man was standing in front, waving his arm and saying something with a stern expression. The blood-stained blacksmith stood beside him looking gloomy. A hum of voices could be heard through the closed window.
"Is my carriage ready?" asked Rostopchin, stepping back from the window.
"It is, your excellency," replied the adjutant.
Rostopchin went again to the balcony door.
"But what do they want?" he asked the superintendent of police.

"Your excellency, they say they've gotten ready, according to your orders, to go fight the French, and they shouted something about treachery. But it's a rowdy crowd, your excellency—I barely managed to get away from them. Your excellency, I'd suggest..."
"You can go. I don't need you to tell me what to do!" Rostopchin snapped angrily.
He stood by the balcony door looking at the crowd.

"This is what they've done with Russia! This is what they've done with me!" he thought, full of an irrepressible fury welling up inside him against someone to whom all of this could be blamed. As often happens with passionate people, he was consumed by anger but was still looking for a target to vent it on. "There's that mob, the dregs of the people," he thought, gazing at the crowd: "this rabble they've stirred up with their stupidity! They want a victim," he thought, looking at the tall young man waving his arm. And this thought came to him precisely because he himself wanted a victim, something on which to vent his rage.
"Is the carriage ready?" he asked again.
"Yes, your excellency. What are your orders about Vereshchagin? He's waiting at the entrance," said the adjutant.
"Ah!" exclaimed Rostopchin, as if struck by an unexpected memory.
And opening the door quickly, he walked out resolutely onto the balcony. The talking instantly stopped, hats and caps came off, and all eyes were raised to the count.

"Good morning, lads!" said the count briskly and loudly. "Thank you for coming. I'll come out to you in a moment, but first we must deal with the villain. We must punish the villain who has caused the ruin of Moscow. Wait for me!"
And the count stepped just as briskly back inside and slammed the door behind him.

A murmur of approval and satisfaction ran through the crowd. "He'll deal with all the villains, you'll see! And you said the French... He'll show you what law is!" the mob was saying, as if reproaching one another for their lack of confidence.

A few minutes later an officer came hurrying out of the front door, gave an order, and the dragoons formed a line. The crowd moved eagerly from the balcony toward the entrance. Rostopchin, coming out there with quick, angry steps, looked hastily around as if searching for someone.

"Where is he?" he asked. And as he spoke, he saw a young man being led around the corner of the house between two dragoons. He had a long thin neck, and his head, which had been half shaved, was again covered with short hair. This young man wore a threadbare blue cloth coat lined with fox fur that had once been elegant, and dirty prison trousers. On his thin, weak legs were heavy chains that hampered his uncertain steps.
"Ah!" said Rostopchin, hurriedly looking away from the young man in the fur-lined coat and pointing to the bottom step of the entrance. "Put him there."

The young man, his chains clanking, stepped clumsily to the spot indicated, holding away with one finger the coat collar that chafed his neck. He turned his long neck this way and that, sighed, and submissively folded his thin hands—hands unused to labor—in front of him.

For several seconds while the young man was taking his place on the step, silence held. Only among the back rows of the people pressing toward the same spot could sighs, groans, and the shuffling of feet be heard.
While waiting for the young man to settle on the step, Rostopchin stood frowning and rubbing his face with his hand.
"Lads!" he said, with a metallic ring in his voice. "This man, Vereshchagin, is the scoundrel who has brought ruin on Moscow."

The young man in the fur-lined coat, stooping slightly, stood in a submissive posture with his fingers clasped before him. His emaciated young face, disfigured by the half-shaven head, hung down hopelessly. At the count's first words he slowly raised it and looked up at him as if wanting to say something, or at least to meet his eyes. But Rostopchin did not look at him. A vein in the young man's long thin neck swelled like a cord and turned blue behind his ear, and suddenly his face flushed.

All eyes were fixed on him. He looked at the crowd, and made somewhat hopeful by the expressions he read on those faces, he smiled sadly and shyly, and lowered his head, shifting his feet on the step.

"He has betrayed his Tsar and his country. He has gone over to Bonaparte. He alone of all Russians has disgraced the Russian name. He has caused Moscow to perish," said Rostopchin in a sharp, even voice, but suddenly he glanced down at Vereshchagin, who continued to stand in the same submissive pose. As if inflamed by the sight, he raised his arm and addressed the people, almost shouting:
"Deal with him as you see fit! I hand him over to you."

The crowd remained silent and only pressed closer and closer together. To hold one another back, to breathe in that stifling atmosphere, to be unable to move, and to await something unknown, incomprehensible, and terrible was becoming unbearable. Those standing in front, who had seen and heard what was happening, all stood with wide-open eyes and mouths, straining with all their strength, holding back the crowd that pushed behind them.
"Beat him! Let the traitor die and not disgrace the Russian name!" shouted Rostopchin. "Cut him down! I command it!"
Hearing not so much the words as the angry tone of Rostopchin's voice, the crowd groaned and surged forward, but stopped again.

"Count!" cried the timid yet dramatic voice of Vereshchagin in the momentary silence that followed. "Count! One God is above us both..." He lifted his head and again the thick vein in his thin neck filled with blood as the color rapidly came and went in his face.
He did not finish what he wanted to say.
"Cut him down! I command it..." shouted Rostopchin, suddenly growing pale like Vereshchagin.
"Draw sabers!" cried the dragoon officer, drawing his own.

Another still stronger wave flowed through the crowd and reaching the front ranks carried it swaying to the very steps of the entrance. The tall youth, with a stony look on his face and a rigid, uplifted arm, stood beside Vereshchagin.
"Saber him!" the dragoon officer almost whispered.
And one of the soldiers, his face suddenly distorted with fury, struck Vereshchagin on the head with the blunt side of his saber.

"Ah!" cried Vereshchagin in meek surprise, looking around with a frightened expression as if not understanding why this was being done to him. A similar gasp of surprise and horror ran through the crowd. "O Lord!" exclaimed a sorrowful voice.

But after the exclamation of surprise that had escaped from Vereshchagin, he uttered a cry of pain, and that cry was fatal. The barrier of human feeling, strained to its utmost, that had held the crowd in check suddenly broke. The crime had begun and had to be completed. The plaintive moan of reproach was drowned by the threatening, angry roar of the crowd. Like the seventh and last wave that shatters a ship, that final irresistible wave burst from the rear and reached the front ranks, sweeping them off their feet and engulfing them all. The dragoon was about to repeat his blow. Vereshchagin, crying out in horror and covering his head with his hands, rushed toward the crowd. The tall youth, against whom he stumbled, seized his thin neck with his hands and, yelling wildly, fell with him under the feet of the pressing, struggling crowd.

Some beat and tore at Vereshchagin, others at the tall youth. And the screams of those being trampled and of those who tried to rescue the tall lad only increased the fury of the crowd. It was a long time before the dragoons could pull out the bleeding youth, beaten almost to death. And for a long time, despite the feverish haste with which the mob tried to finish the work it had begun, those who were hitting, strangling, and tearing at Vereshchagin could not kill him, because the crowd pressed from all sides, swaying as one mass with them in the center, making it impossible either to kill him or let him go.
"Hit him with an ax, eh!... Crushed?... Traitor, he sold Christ... Still alive... stubborn... serves him right! Use the hatchet!... What—still alive?"

Only when the victim ceased to struggle and his cries changed to a long, measured death rattle did the crowd around his prostrate, bleeding corpse begin rapidly to change places. Each person came up, glanced at what had been done, and with horror, reproach, and astonishment pushed back again.

"O Lord! The people are like wild beasts! How could he still be alive?" voices in the crowd could be heard saying. "Quite a young fellow too... must have been a merchant's son. What men!... and they say he's not the right one... How not the right one?... O Lord! And there's another one who's been beaten too—they say he's nearly done for... Oh, the people... Aren't they afraid of sinning?..." said the same mob now, looking with pained distress at the dead body with its long, thin, half-severed neck and its livid face stained with blood and dust.

A careful police officer, finding the presence of a corpse in his excellency's courtyard unseemly, told the dragoons to take it away. Two dragoons grabbed it by its distorted legs and dragged it along the ground. The gory, dust-stained, half-shaven head with its long neck trailed twisting along the ground. The crowd shrank back from it.

At the moment Vereshchagin fell and the crowd closed in with savage yells, Rostopchin suddenly turned pale and, instead of going to the back entrance where his carriage was waiting, hurried with bent head along the corridor leading to the rooms on the ground floor, not knowing where he was going or why. The count's face was white and he could not control the feverish twitching of his lower jaw.
"This way, your excellency... Where are you going?... This way, please..." said a trembling, frightened voice behind him.

Count Rostopchin was unable to reply and, turning obediently, went in the direction indicated. At the back entrance stood his carriage. The distant roar of the yelling crowd was audible even there. He hastily got in and told the coachman to drive him to his country house in Sokolniki.

When they reached Myasnitsky Street and could no longer hear the shouts of the mob, the count began to feel remorse. He remembered with dissatisfaction the agitation and fear he had shown before his subordinates. "The mob is terrible—disgusting," he said to himself in French. "They are like wolves that only flesh can satisfy." "Count! One God is above us both!"—Vereshchagin's words suddenly came back to him, and an unpleasant shiver ran down his back. But this was only a momentary feeling, and Count Rostopchin smiled scornfully at himself. "I had other duties," he thought. "The people had to be calmed. Many other victims have perished and are perishing for the public good"—and he began thinking of his social duties to his family and to the city entrusted to him, and of himself—not himself as Theodore Vasilyevich Rostopchin (he imagined that Theodore Vasilyevich Rostopchin was sacrificing himself for the public good) but himself as governor, the representative of authority and of the Tsar. "Had I been simply Theodore Vasilyevich, my course of action would have been quite different, but it was my duty to safeguard my life and dignity as commander in chief."

Gently swaying on the flexible springs of his carriage and no longer hearing the terrible sounds of the crowd, Rostopchin grew physically calm and, as always happens, as soon as he became physically calm his mind found reasons why he should be mentally calm too. The thought that calmed Rostopchin was not a new one. Since the world began and men have killed one another, no one has ever committed such a crime against a fellow human without comforting himself with this same idea. This idea is the public good—the hypothetical welfare of other people.
For a person not driven by passion, that welfare is never certain, but the one who commits such a crime always knows exactly where that welfare lies. And Rostopchin now knew it.

Not only did his reason not reproach him for what he had done, but he even found cause for satisfaction in having so successfully seized a convenient opportunity to punish a criminal while also pacifying the mob.

"Vereshchagin was tried and condemned to death," thought Rostopchin (though the Senate had only sentenced Vereshchagin to hard labor). "He was a traitor and a spy. I could not let him go unpunished, and so I killed two birds with one stone: I gave the mob a victim to calm them, and I punished a criminal."
Having reached his country house and begun giving orders about household arrangements, the count grew quite calm.

Half an hour later he was driving with fast horses across the Sokolniki field, no longer thinking of what had happened but considering what was still to come. He was heading to the Yauza bridge, where he had heard that Kutuzov was. Count Rostopchin was mentally preparing the angry, stinging reproaches he intended to deliver to Kutuzov for his deception. He would make that sly old courtier feel that the responsibility for all the calamities following the abandonment of the city and the ruin of Russia (as Rostopchin saw it) would fall on his senile old head. Planning what he would say to Kutuzov, Rostopchin angrily turned in his carriage and gazed sternly from side to side.

The Sokolniki field was deserted. Only at the far end, in front of the almshouse and the lunatic asylum, could some people in white be seen, and others like them walking alone across the field, shouting and gesturing.

One of these was running to cross the path of Count Rostopchin's carriage, and the count himself, his coachman, and his dragoons all looked with vague horror and curiosity at these released lunatics, especially at the one running toward them.

Swaying from side to side on his long, thin legs in his fluttering dressing gown, this madman was running straight at Rostopchin, shouting something in a hoarse voice and making signs for him to stop. The lunatic's solemn, gloomy face was thin and yellow, with its beard growing in uneven tufts. His black pupils with saffron-yellow whites moved restlessly near the lower eyelids.
"Stop! Pull up, I tell you!" he cried in a piercing voice, and again shouted something breathlessly with emphatic gestures.
Coming alongside the carriage, he ran beside it.

"Three times have they slain me, three times have I risen from the dead. They stoned me, crucified me... I shall rise... shall rise... shall rise. They have torn my body. The kingdom of God will be overthrown... Three times will I overthrow it and three times re-establish it!" he cried, raising his voice higher and higher.

Count Rostopchin suddenly grew pale as he had done when the crowd closed in on Vereshchagin. He turned away. "Go fas... faster!" he cried in a trembling voice to his coachman. The carriage flew over the ground as fast as the horses could pull it, but for a long time Count Rostopchin still heard the insane, despairing screams growing fainter in the distance, while his eyes saw nothing but the astonished, frightened, bloodstained face of "the traitor" in the fur-lined coat.

Recent as that image was, Rostopchin already felt that it had cut deep into his heart and drawn blood. Even now he felt clearly that the bloody trace of that memory would not fade with time, but that the terrible recollection would, on the contrary, dwell in his heart ever more cruelly and painfully to the end of his life. He seemed still to hear the sound of his own words: "Cut him down! I command it..."

"Why did I say those words? It was by some accident I said them... I didn't need to say them," he thought. "And then nothing would have happened." He saw the frightened and then furious face of the dragoon who dealt the blow, the look of silent, timid reproach that boy in the fur-lined coat had turned upon him. "But I didn't do it for my own sake. I was obligated to act that way... The mob, the traitor... the public welfare," thought he.

Troops were still crowding at the Yauza bridge. It was hot. Kutuzov, dejected and frowning, sat on a bench by the bridge toying with his riding whip in the sand when a carriage dashed up noisily. A man in a general's uniform with plumes in his hat went up to Kutuzov and said something in French. It was Count Rostopchin. He told Kutuzov that he had come because Moscow, the capital, was no more and only the army remained.
"Things would have been different if your Serene Highness had not told me that you would not abandon Moscow without another battle; all this would not have happened," he said.

Kutuzov looked at Rostopchin as if, not grasping what was being said to him, he was trying to read something peculiar written at that moment on the face of the man addressing him. Rostopchin grew confused and fell silent. Kutuzov slightly shook his head and, without taking his penetrating gaze from Rostopchin's face, muttered softly:
"No! I shall not give up Moscow without a battle!"

Whether Kutuzov was thinking of something entirely different when he spoke those words, or uttered them purposely knowing them to be meaningless, Rostopchin made no reply and hurriedly left him. And strange to say, the Governor of Moscow, the proud Count Rostopchin, picked up a Cossack whip and went to the bridge, where he began shouting and driving away the carts that blocked the way.

title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The human mind cannot grasp the causes of events in their totality, but the desire to find those causes is planted deep in the human soul. Without considering the countless complexity of conditions—any one of which, taken alone, might seem to be the cause—a person seizes on the first explanation that seems intelligible and says: 'This is the cause!' In historical events, the first and most primitive explanation was the will of the gods, and after that, the will of those who stood in the most prominent positions—the heroes of history. But we need only look beneath the surface of any historical event—which really lies in the activity of the masses who take part in it—to see that the will of the historical hero doesn't control the actions of the masses, but is itself constantly controlled. It may seem unimportant whether we understand historical events one way or another. Yet there is the same difference between someone who says 'the peoples of the West moved eastward because Napoleon wished it' and someone who says 'this happened because it had to happen,' as between those who believed the earth was stationary and the planets revolved around it, and those who admitted they didn't know what held the earth in place but knew there were laws governing its motion. There is, and can be, no cause of a historical event except the one cause of all causes. But there are laws directing events, and some of these laws we know while others we cannot yet comprehend. Discovering these laws becomes possible only when we completely abandon the attempt to find the cause in the will of any single individual, just as the laws of planetary motion were discovered only when people abandoned the idea that the earth was fixed.

Historians consider that, next to the Battle of Borodino and the occupation and burning of Moscow, the most important episode of the 1812 war was the movement of the Russian army from the Ryazan to the Kaluga road and to the Tarutino camp—the so-called flank march across the Krasnaya Pakhra River. They attribute this stroke of genius to various individuals and debate who deserves the credit. Even foreign historians, including the French, acknowledge the genius of the Russian commanders when they discuss this flank march. But it's hard to understand why military writers, and others following them, consider this maneuver to be some brilliant conception by a single man who saved Russia and destroyed Napoleon. First, it's hard to see where the genius lay, because it didn't take much brainpower to see that the best position for an army not under attack is where supplies are most plentiful—even a dull thirteen-year-old could have guessed that the best position after the retreat from Moscow was on the Kaluga road. So it's impossible to understand how historians conclude this was a profound maneuver. And it's even harder to understand why they think it saved Russia and destroyed the French, since this flank march—had it been preceded, accompanied, or followed by other circumstances—might have proved ruinous for the Russians. If the Russian army's position did begin to improve after this march, it doesn't follow at all that the march was the cause.

That flank march might not only have failed to benefit the Russian army but, under other circumstances, could have led to its destruction. What would have happened if Moscow hadn't burned down? If Murat hadn't lost sight of the Russians? If Napoleon hadn't remained inactive? If the Russian army at Krasnaya Pakhra had given battle, as Bennigsen and Barclay advised? What if the French had attacked the Russians while they were marching beyond the Pakhra? What if Napoleon had attacked the Russians approaching Tarutino with even a tenth of the energy he showed at Smolensk? What if the French had marched on Petersburg? In any of these scenarios, the flank march that supposedly brought salvation might have proved disastrous.

The third and most baffling thing is that historians studying this period deliberately avoid acknowledging that this flank march cannot be attributed to any single person, that no one foresaw it, and that in reality—like the retreat from Fili—it never occurred to anyone as a complete plan.
