It emerged moment by moment, step by step, event by event, from an endless number of diverse circumstances, and was only seen as a whole after it was accomplished and belonged to the past.

At the council at Fili, the prevailing idea among the Russian commanders was the most natural one: a direct retreat along the Nizhni road. Proof of this lies in the fact that the majority voted for such a retreat, and especially in the well-known conversation after the council between the commander in chief and Lanskoy, who was in charge of supplies. Lanskoy informed the commander in chief that army provisions were mostly stored along the Oka River in the Tula and Ryazan provinces, and that retreating toward Nizhni would separate the army from its supplies by the broad Oka, which can't be crossed early in winter. This was the first indication that they needed to deviate from the most natural course—a direct retreat toward Nizhni-Novgorod. The army turned more to the south, along the Ryazan road and closer to its supplies. Later, the French inactivity (they even lost sight of the Russian army), concern for the arsenal at Tula, and the advantage of moving closer to provisions caused the army to turn still further south onto the Tula road. After crossing to the Tula road beyond the Pakhra by a forced march, the Russian commanders planned to stay at Podolsk and had no thought of the Tarutino position. But countless circumstances—the reappearance of French troops, plans for giving battle, and above all the abundance of food in Kaluga province—forced the army to turn even further south, crossing from the Tula to the Kaluga road and proceeding to Tarutino, which lay between the supply routes. Just as it's impossible to say when the decision was made to abandon Moscow, it's impossible to say precisely when, or by whom, the decision was made to move to Tarutino. Only when the army had arrived there, as the result of innumerable and varying forces, did people begin assuring themselves that they had planned this movement all along and had foreseen its outcome.

title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Regarding military matters, Napoleon immediately upon entering Moscow gave General Sebastiani strict orders to monitor the Russian army's movements, sent army corps along the various roads, and instructed Murat to find Kutuzov. Then he carefully oversaw the fortification of the Kremlin and drew up a brilliant plan for a future campaign covering the entire map of Russia.

In diplomatic affairs, Napoleon summoned Captain Yakovlev—who had been robbed, was dressed in rags, and had no idea how to get out of Moscow—and explained his entire policy and his magnanimity in great detail. Having written a letter to Emperor Alexander in which he felt duty-bound to inform his Friend and Brother that Rostopchin had badly mismanaged things in Moscow, he dispatched Yakovlev to Petersburg.
Having similarly explained his views and his magnanimity to Tutolmin, he sent that old man off to Petersburg to negotiate as well.
In legal matters, immediately after the fires, he ordered that the arsonists be found and executed. And the 'scoundrel' Rostopchin was punished by an order to burn down his houses.
In administrative affairs, Moscow was granted a constitution. A municipal government was established and the following announcement issued:
CITIZENS OF MOSCOW!

Your misfortunes are terrible, but His Majesty the Emperor and King wishes to end them. Harsh examples have shown you how he punishes disobedience and crime. Strict measures have been taken to restore order and public safety. A fatherly administration, chosen from among yourselves, will form your municipal government. It will care for you, your needs, and your welfare. Its members will be marked by a red ribbon worn across the shoulder, and the mayor will also wear a white belt. But when not on duty, they will wear only a red ribbon on the left arm.

The city police has been restored on its former basis, and its activity has already improved public order. The government has appointed two commissaries general, or police chiefs, and twenty ward commissioners to the city's different districts. You will know them by the white ribbon on their left arm. Several churches of various denominations are open, and services continue without interference. Your fellow citizens are returning daily, and orders have been given that they shall find help and protection in their homes. These are the government's measures to restore order and ease your condition. But to achieve this, you must add your own efforts: forget, if possible, the misfortunes you've suffered; trust in a less cruel fate; be certain that inevitable, shameful death awaits anyone who threatens your persons or your remaining property; and have no doubt that your safety is assured, for such is the will of the greatest and most just of monarchs. Soldiers and citizens, whatever your nation—restore public trust, the foundation of a state's welfare. Live as brothers, give each other aid and protection, unite to resist the evil-minded, obey the military and civil authorities, and your tears will soon dry!
Regarding army provisions, Napoleon decreed that all troops should take turns entering Moscow to forage—'à la maraude'—so the army could provide for itself.
(That is, as looters.)
Regarding religion, Napoleon ordered the priests brought back and services resumed in the churches.
Regarding trade and army supplies, the following was posted everywhere:
PROCLAMATION

You, peaceful citizens of Moscow, artisans and workers driven from the city by misfortune, and you scattered farmers still kept from your fields by groundless fear—listen! Peace is returning to this capital and order is being restored. Your countrymen are emerging boldly from hiding, finding they are treated with respect. Any violence to them or their property is promptly punished. His Majesty the Emperor and King protects them and considers none of you his enemy except those who disobey his orders. He wishes to end your suffering and return you to your homes and families. Come to us without fear. Citizens, return confidently to your dwellings! You will soon find ways to meet your needs. Craftsmen and industrious workers, return to your trades, your homes, your shops, where guards await to protect you! You will receive proper pay for your work. And you, peasants—come out of the forests where you hide in terror. Return to your villages without fear, knowing you will find protection! Markets have been set up in the city where you may bring your surplus produce. The government has ensured free trade through the following measures: (1) Starting today, farmers and those living near Moscow may safely bring supplies of all kinds to two designated markets—one on Mokhovaya Street and the other at the Provision Market. (2) Goods will be purchased at prices agreed between buyer and seller, and if a seller cannot get a fair price, he may freely take his goods home—no one may hinder him. (3) Sundays and Wednesdays are the main market days, with sufficient troops stationed along the highways on Tuesdays and Saturdays to protect supply carts. (4) Similar measures will protect peasants returning with their carts. (5) Steps will be taken immediately to restore normal trade.

Citizens and villagers, workers and artisans of all nations—you are called to carry out the fatherly intentions of His Majesty the Emperor and King and to work with him for the common good! Place your trust at his feet and join us without delay!

To raise the spirits of both troops and civilians, reviews were constantly held and rewards distributed. The Emperor rode through the streets to comfort the residents and, despite his preoccupation with state affairs, personally attended the theaters he had ordered to be set up.

In matters of philanthropy—the supreme virtue of crowned heads—Napoleon did everything in his power. He had the words 'House of My Mother' inscribed on charitable institutions, blending tender filial devotion with a monarch's majestic generosity. He visited the Foundling Hospital and, allowing the orphans he had 'saved' to kiss his white hands, conversed graciously with Tutolmin. Then, as Thiers eloquently recounts, he ordered his soldiers to be paid in forged Russian currency he had prepared: 'Ennobling the use of these means by an act worthy of himself and of the French army, he had relief distributed to fire victims. But as food was too precious to give to foreigners—most of whom were enemies—Napoleon preferred to supply them with money to buy food from outside, and had paper rubles distributed to them.'
Regarding military discipline, orders were continually issued imposing severe punishment for neglect of duty and to suppress looting.

title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Four weeks had passed since Pierre had been taken prisoner. Though the French had offered to transfer him from the soldiers' shed to the officers' quarters, he had stayed in the shed where he'd first been placed.

In burned and devastated Moscow, Pierre experienced nearly the furthest limits of deprivation a person can endure. But thanks to his physical strength and health—which he'd been unaware of until now—and especially because the hardships came so gradually that it was impossible to say when they began, he bore his situation not only easily but even joyfully. And it was precisely now that he found the peace of mind and inner harmony he had previously strived for in vain. He had long sought it in different ways—in philanthropy, in Freemasonry, in the distractions of city life, in wine, in heroic self-sacrifice, and in his romantic love for Natasha. He had sought it through reason—and all these attempts had failed him. Now, without thinking about it, he had found that peace and inner harmony only through the horror of death, through deprivation, and through what he recognized in Karataev.

Those terrible moments he had lived through at the executions had washed away from his mind, as if forever, the anxious thoughts and feelings that had once seemed so important. It no longer occurred to him to think about Russia, or the war, or politics, or Napoleon. It was obvious to him that none of these were his concern, that he had no business judging them, and therefore couldn't. 'Russia and summer weather don't come tied together,' he thought, repeating Karataev's words, which he found strangely comforting. His intention of killing Napoleon and his calculations about the number of the Beast in Revelation now seemed meaningless and even ridiculous. His anger at his wife, his worry about his name being dishonored—these seemed not just trivial but amusing. What did it matter to him that some woman somewhere was living as she pleased? What did it matter to anyone, especially him, whether they discovered that their prisoner's name was Count Bezukhov?

He now often recalled his conversation with Prince Andrew and completely agreed with him, though he understood Andrew's thoughts somewhat differently. Prince Andrew had said that happiness could only be negative, but he'd said it with a shade of bitterness and irony, as though he were really saying that the desire for positive happiness is planted in us only to torment us and never be satisfied. But Pierre believed this without any mental reservation. The absence of suffering, the satisfaction of one's needs, and the consequent freedom to choose one's occupation—that is, one's way of life—now seemed to Pierre to be unquestionably the highest human happiness. Here and now, for the first time, he fully appreciated the pleasure of eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, sleeping when tired, warmth when cold, and talking to another person when he wanted to hear a human voice. The satisfaction of one's needs—good food, cleanliness, freedom—now that he was deprived of all this, seemed to Pierre to constitute perfect happiness. And the choice of occupation—now that this was so restricted—seemed such a simple matter that he forgot how an excess of life's comforts destroys the joy of meeting one's needs, and how great freedom in choosing one's path—the kind his wealth, education, and social position had given him—is exactly what makes that choice impossibly difficult and kills the desire and ability to have any occupation at all.

All Pierre's daydreams now centered on the time when he would be free. Yet for the rest of his life, he thought and spoke with deep feeling about that month of captivity—those irretrievable, powerful, joyful sensations, and above all the complete peace of mind and inner freedom he experienced only during those weeks.

When on the first day he rose early, stepped out of the shed at dawn, and saw the domes and crosses of the New Convent of the Virgin still dark against the sky, the hoarfrost on the dusty grass, the Sparrow Hills, and the wooded banks above the winding river fading into the purple distance; when he felt the touch of fresh air and heard the crows flying from Moscow across the field; and when light flared from the east and the sun's rim appeared solemnly from behind a cloud, and the domes and crosses, the frost, the distance, and the river all began to sparkle in the joyful light—Pierre felt a new strength and joy in life such as he had never known. And this feeling not only stayed with him throughout his imprisonment but even grew stronger as his hardships increased.

That alertness and readiness for anything was further strengthened by the high opinion his fellow prisoners formed of him soon after his arrival. His knowledge of languages, the respect the French showed him, his simplicity, his willingness to give away anything asked of him (he received the officers' allowance of three rubles a week), his strength (which he demonstrated by pressing nails into the hut's walls), his gentleness toward his companions, and his ability to sit still and think without doing anything (which struck them as mysterious)—all this gave him an almost heroic status among them. The very qualities that had been a hindrance, even harmful, in his former world—his strength, his indifference to comfort, his absent-mindedness and simplicity—here, among these people, made him nearly a hero. And Pierre felt that their opinion placed responsibilities on him.

title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: The French evacuation began on the night between the sixth and seventh of October: kitchens and sheds were dismantled, carts loaded, and troops and baggage trains set off.

At seven in the morning, a French convoy in marching order—wearing shakos and carrying muskets, knapsacks, and enormous sacks—stood in front of the sheds. Animated French conversation mixed with curses sounded along the entire line.

In the shed, everyone was ready—dressed, belted, and wearing shoes—waiting only for the order to start. Only the sick soldier Sokolov, pale and thin with dark circles under his eyes, sat barefoot and undressed in his place. His eyes, prominent from the thinness of his face, gazed questioningly at his comrades, who paid no attention to him. He moaned regularly and quietly. It was clearly not so much his suffering that made him moan (he had dysentery) as his fear and grief at being left behind.
Pierre, with a rope tied around his waist and wearing shoes Karataev had made him from leather torn off a tea chest by a French soldier, went up to the sick man and crouched beside him.
'You know, Sokolov, they're not all leaving. There's a hospital here. You might actually be better off than the rest of us,' said Pierre.
'Oh Lord! Oh, it'll be the death of me! Oh Lord!' the man moaned louder.
'I'll go ask them again right now,' said Pierre, standing up and going to the shed door.

Just as Pierre reached the door, the corporal who had offered him a pipe the day before came up with two soldiers. The corporal and soldiers were in marching gear—knapsacks and shakos with metal chin straps—and these accessories made their familiar faces look completely different.
The corporal had come, on orders, to shut the door. The prisoners had to be counted before being let out.
'Corporal, what will they do with the sick man?...' Pierre began.

But even as he spoke, he began to doubt whether this was really the corporal he knew, or a stranger—so unlike himself did the man seem at that moment. Moreover, just as Pierre spoke, a sharp rattle of drums suddenly burst out from both sides. The corporal frowned at Pierre's words and, muttering some meaningless oaths, slammed the door shut. The shed went dark, and the sharp drum rattle drowned out the sick man's groans from both sides.

'There it is!... That force again!...' Pierre said to himself, and an involuntary shudder ran down his spine. In the corporal's transformed face, in the sound of his voice, in the stirring, deafening noise of the drums, Pierre recognized that mysterious, cold force that compelled people against their will to kill their fellow men—the force he had witnessed during the executions. To fear it, to try to escape it, to plead with or preach to those who served as its instruments was useless. Pierre understood this now. One could only wait and endure. He didn't go back to the sick man or turn to look at him, but stood frowning by the shed door.

When the door was opened and the prisoners, pressing against one another like a flock of sheep, squeezed through the exit, Pierre pushed forward and approached the very captain whom the corporal had assured him would do anything for him. The captain was also in marching gear, and on his cold face Pierre recognized that same force he had seen in the corporal's words and in the roll of the drums.
'Move along, move along!' the captain repeated, frowning sternly and scanning the prisoners streaming past him.
Pierre went up to him, though he knew the attempt would be useless.
'What is it?' the officer asked coldly, as if not recognizing Pierre.
Pierre told him about the sick man.
'He can walk, damn him!' said the captain. 'Move along, move along!' he continued without looking at Pierre.
'But he's dying,' Pierre began again.
'Would you be so good as to—' the captain shouted, his face darkening with anger.
'Drum-da-da-dum, dum-dum...' rattled the drums, and Pierre understood that this mysterious force had total control over these men and that there was no point saying anything more.
The officer prisoners were separated from the soldiers and told to march in front. There were about thirty officers, Pierre among them, and about three hundred soldiers.

The officers, who had come from other sheds, were all strangers to Pierre and much better dressed. They looked at him and his shoes with suspicion, as if he were an outsider. Not far from him walked a fat major with a sallow, bloated, angry face, wearing a Kazan dressing gown tied with a towel. He clearly commanded respect among his fellow prisoners. He kept one hand, clutching his tobacco pouch, inside the front of his dressing gown and held the stem of his pipe firmly with the other. Panting and puffing, the major grumbled at everyone, convinced he was being pushed and that they were all hurrying for no reason and amazed at nothing worth being amazed about. Another man, a thin little officer, talked to everyone, speculating about where they were being taken and how far they'd march that day. An official in felt boots and a commissariat uniform ran from side to side, pointing at the ruins of Moscow and loudly announcing what had burned and identifying different parts of the city. A third officer, a Pole by his accent, argued with the commissariat man about which neighborhood was which.

'What's the point of arguing?' said the major angrily. 'What does it matter if it's St. Nicholas or St. Blaise? It's burned down, and that's the end of it. What are you pushing for? Isn't the road wide enough?' he snapped at someone behind him who wasn't pushing at all.

'Oh, oh, oh! Look what they've done!' the prisoners murmured on all sides, gazing at the charred ruins. 'Everything beyond the river, and Zubovo, and the Kremlin... Just look! Not half of it left. Yes, I told you—the whole district beyond the river. That's how it is.'
'Well, you can see it's burned. What's the use of talking about it?' said the major.
As they passed a church in the Khamovniki district—one of the few unburned parts of Moscow—the whole crowd of prisoners suddenly recoiled, and exclamations of horror and disgust were heard.
'Oh, the monsters! What heathens! Yes—dead, dead he is... And his face is smeared with something!'

Pierre pushed forward toward the church where this sight was causing such outrage, and dimly made out something propped against the fence around the churchyard. From his companions who could see better, he learned it was a dead body, set upright against the railings with its face smeared with soot.
'Move on! What the devil... Move on! Thirty thousand devils!...' the guards cursed, and the French soldiers drove the crowd of staring prisoners away with fresh viciousness, swords in hand.

title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: One of the most obvious and effective departures from the so-called rules of war is the action of scattered groups against massed formations. This kind of fighting always arises in wars that take on a national character. In such actions, instead of two armies facing each other in formation, men disperse, attack individually, run when confronted by stronger forces, and attack again when the opportunity presents itself. This is what the guerrillas did in Spain, what the mountain tribes did in the Caucasus, and what the Russians did in 1812.

People have called this 'guerrilla warfare' and assume that by naming it they've explained it. But this kind of war fits no established rules and directly contradicts a widely accepted tactical principle that an attacker should concentrate his forces to be stronger than his opponent at the moment of contact.
Guerrilla warfare—which has always been successful, as history shows—directly violates that rule.
This contradiction arises because military science equates an army's strength with its numbers. Military science says: more troops means more strength. 'Big battalions are always right.'
(Large battalions are always victorious.)
For military science to say this is like defining momentum in mechanics by mass alone—claiming that momenta are equal or unequal simply because the masses are equal or unequal.
Momentum—quantity of motion—is the product of mass and velocity.
In military affairs, an army's strength is the product of its mass and some unknown factor, x.

Military science, observing countless historical instances where army size doesn't correspond to actual strength—where small detachments defeat larger ones—vaguely acknowledges this unknown factor and tries to identify it: sometimes in formations, sometimes in equipment, and most often in the genius of commanders. But assigning these meanings to the factor never produces results that match the historical facts.
Yet we need only abandon the false view—adopted to flatter 'heroes'—that the orders issued by wartime commanders actually determine outcomes, and this unknown quantity reveals itself.

That unknown quantity is the spirit of the army: the greater or lesser willingness to fight and face danger felt by every man in the army, regardless of whether they serve under a genius, fight in two or three lines, or carry cudgels or rifles that fire thirty rounds a minute. Men who want to fight will always find the most advantageous conditions for fighting.
The spirit of an army is the factor which, multiplied by its mass, yields the resulting force. Defining and measuring this unknown factor—the spirit of an army—is a problem for science.

This problem can only be solved if we stop arbitrarily substituting for x the conditions under which it becomes visible—such as the general's commands, the equipment used, and so forth—mistaking these for the thing itself. We must recognize this unknown in its entirety as the greater or lesser desire to fight and to face danger. Only then, by expressing known historical facts as equations and comparing the relative significance of this factor, can we hope to define the unknown.

Ten men, battalions, or divisions fighting fifteen conquer them—that is, kill or capture them all—while themselves losing four. So on one side four were lost and on the other fifteen. Therefore the four equaled the fifteen, meaning 4x = 15y, and x/y = 15/4. This equation doesn't give us the value of the unknown, but it gives us a ratio between two unknowns. By applying various historical units—battles, campaigns, periods of war—to such equations, a series of numbers could be obtained that might reveal certain laws.

The tactical rule that an army should mass when attacking and spread out when retreating unconsciously confirms the truth that an army's strength depends on its spirit. To lead men forward under fire requires more discipline (achievable only through mass movement) than defending against an attack. But this rule, which ignores the army's spirit, proves consistently wrong—especially when the spirit of the troops rises or falls sharply, as in all national wars.

The French, retreating in 1812, should according to tactics have broken into smaller groups to defend themselves, but instead they clustered into a mass because their spirit had fallen so low that only the mass held the army together. The Russians, who according to tactics should have attacked in mass, instead split into small units, because their spirit had risen so high that individual men, without orders, struck at the French and willingly exposed themselves to hardship and danger without needing anyone to compel them.
